translations.text: The Ladder of virtues that leads up to heaven, spoken by Daniel, monk of Raithu, concerning this book, the enlightener of souls, which is called Climax, that is, Ladder. Those who wish to have their names written in the book of life in heaven, and who hasten to ascend toward the good things of heavenly blessedness, let this holy book show them a good pattern and teaching for their course. And those who read it will find an unerring guide, who leads all who follow him toward the kingdom of heaven and keeps them from stumbling on any of the stones that cause stumbling. It will become for them a ladder raised from earth to heaven, leading from earth to that holy one, which shows God standing upon its top. And it is like that ladder which Jacob, the trampler of the passions, once saw as he rested on the bed of ascetic struggle. Therefore I beseech you, brothers, let us too ascend, with faith and love, this spiritual ladder that leads up to heaven, whose first step teaches us well. On renunciation of this vain world. On hatred of the world and its affairs. On estrangement, in which it speaks also of empty dreams. On the martyrdom that comes about through obedience. On repentance, in which it speaks of the prison.

On the remembrance of death. On the mourning that cleanses sins. On freedom from anger. On the remembrance of wrongs. On evil-speaking. On silence. On lying. On despondency. On gluttony. On fornication. On love of money. On poverty. On hardness of heart. On singing in the assemblies. On vigilance. On cowardice. On vainglory. On pride, in which it speaks also of blasphemy. On gentleness and simplicity. On humility. On discernment and understanding. On stillness and withdrawal and the guarding of the mind. On prayer with a collected mind. On dispassion. On love and faith and hope. The God-clad father John strove well and gathered all the work of the monastic life into this book. And he made the number of these spiritual steps correspond to the years of the Lord's bodily age, for at thirty years of age the Lord Jesus Christ was baptized; and so this man has depicted for us a ladder of thirty ascents, and if we reach its top we shall be from then on

perfect and unfalling. But whoever has not yet been perfected on this Ladder is an infant, useless and untrustworthy for every testimony of the heart. And we have thought it necessary first to set down here briefly the life of this all-wise man, according to my ability and as far as I attain to knowledge, so that we may see his labors and not become unbelieving of his words.

Epistle of the holy father John, abbot of Raithu, to the blessed John, abbot of Sinai.

To the one blessed in God, the equal of the angels, the father of fathers and teacher of us all: the sinner John, abbot of Raithu. Greetings in the Lord. We poor ones know your unwavering obedience, together with all your other virtues, and most of all where it is a matter of the increase and multiplying of the talent given to you by God. For this reason we write to your holiness, according to the word of Scripture which says: "Ask your father and he will tell you, and your elders will inform you." For this reason, as to the common father of all, an elder greater than all in both ascetic struggle and learning, and a good teacher, we beseech the height of your virtues to write to us, unlearned as we are, what you have seen on that same mountain in your vision of God, like the great Moses. And as on spiritual tablets, let them inscribe the book written by you for the instruction of this new Israel, those who have only now come out from the invisible Egyptians and from the sea of this world. And just as, with that God-speaking tongue of yours in place of a staff, and by the grace of God, you have worked many miracles and have saved many from the sea of this world, so now too, we beseech you, do not count us unworthy, but write out well, with the Lord's help, as a great teacher, what befits the life of monks, for all who have entered this angelic way of life.
And do not think that we speak these words with any guile or insincerity, for you know, holy father, that

such a thing is far from us; rather, we speak as is true and as is believed by all. Therefore we trust in God that we shall soon receive the spiritual tablets we are awaiting, so that they may lead without error all who follow them; and so that those teachings may be like a ladder leading up to the gates of heaven for all who follow them and hasten to ascend there, and so that through your teaching they may pass unhindered by the evil spirits, the world-rulers of darkness and the princes of the air. For if Jacob was a shepherd of sheep and saw such an awesome vision upon that ladder, how much more should you, who are a shepherd of rational sheep, show us the unerring way to God, not only by vision but in deed and in truth. Farewell in the Lord, honored and holy father.

Epistle of the holy and blessed John, abbot of Sinai, to which this writing, the Spiritual Tablets, belongs.

John greets John. Your honored letter has reached us, which was just as befitted your passionless and virtue-filled life and your holy and humble heart. You wrote to us poor ones virtuously, for just as your holiness is always accustomed to give us an example of humility, so for this reason you have done this too, in that you have asked from us, who are unlearned in both deed and word, a word of teaching, and have commanded of us a task beyond our strength. But I say this, that if there were not upon me the fear of the mother

...from it, of all the virtues, which is obedience, lest I cast off its yoke from me, I would not have dared a task beyond my strength. For it was fitting for you, O wondrous father, if you inquire into such matters, to learn them from those who know well the work of virtue, for we are still at the measure of disciples and not of teachers. But the God-clad fathers and teachers of obedience say that obedience is this: that a person should undertake, without wavering, tasks beyond his strength at the word of his superiors. For this reason I have, in humility, undertaken a task beyond my strength, not that what I say here might be of any use to you. For I too know, O holy father, as do all who possess wisdom of mind, that your mind is pure of all the darkness of the passions, goes unhindered to the divine light, and is illumined by it. But because I feared the death that comes from disobedience, I came to obey your holy command, with fear and with longing, as an obedient and faithful servant, poor and useless, of a skilled painter. With this small and worthless understanding of mine, and with a thin voice and speech, I have sketched the living words in ink alone, and I have left it to you, O leader of teachers, to adorn well and bring to clarity what I have sketched, and to complete all that is lacking, as the perfecter of spiritual tablets. But, as I said, it is not as teaching for you that I have offered this writing, far from it, for you, holy one, are able to teach and confirm many, and even ourselves, in divine matters and teachings,
but I have written it for that divine congregation

which is with us under obedience to you, O teacher of teachers! For its sake, through your prayers and theirs and through hope in the Lord, I have been lightened a little of the weight of my ignorance, and I have raised the sail of my pen and given the rudder of our speech into the hands of your prayers. I begin to speak at your word. And I ask of all who come upon these words spoken by me: if anyone finds any profit in these words, reckon its fruit to this our holy father, who commanded us to do this, and pray for me only for the effort. Do not look at these words, for they are truly worthless and full of every kind of ignorance. Therefore pray for me on account of my zeal, for God gives the reward not according to the abundance of gifts and labors, but according to the abundance of zeal. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
The teachings of our holy and blessed father John, abbot of Sinai, which he dedicated to Father John, abbot of Raithu, for he had asked him to write down teachings for monks.

Chapter One: On Departure from the World. 1. With the help of our good, man-loving, and merciful God and King, let us begin the discourse, for it is good that we make God the beginning of a discourse addressed to the servants of God. For all whom that good and glorious God created are rational, and he honored them with free will. Because of this, some are his friends, some faithful servants, some useless servants, some wholly estranged, and others, though they are powerless, are even his opponents. Now by friends of God we unlearned ones understand, O holy father, those incorporeal and intelligible natures that surround him; by faithful servants, all who diligently do his will; and by useless servants, all who have received baptism and have not faithfully kept the vows they made to God in baptism. 2. And by strangers and enemies of God we understand those who are either unbaptized and unbelieving

or who believe wrongly; and the combatants and opponents are those who have not only cast off the fear of the Lord from themselves, but who also fiercely fight and oppose all who do the will of God. And since a separate and proper discourse belongs to each of all these whom we have mentioned, and we poor and unlearned ones are unable to speak about all of them individually, therefore let us come to those faithful servants of God, who have rightly compelled the unworthy one,

to stretch out our hand in unwavering obedience. From their understanding let us take the pen of our discourse, and let us dip it, as if in ink, in their sorrowing and radiant humility; and upon their hearts, polished and made white by virtue, as upon sheets of paper, or rather as upon spiritual tablets, let us begin to write those divine words and seeds of virtue, and let us speak thus: 3. God is found by all who desire and seek him, for he is the God of all and the life of all: of unbelievers and believers, of the righteous and sinners, of the dispassionate and the passionate, of the pious and the impious, of laypeople and monks, of the wise and the unlearned, of the healthy and the weak, of the young and the old. Just as the expanse of light, the sight of the sun, and the nature of the air are over all, so he is the life of all and the giver of all this, and those who seek him find him, for there is no change in him, nor any partiality before God.

4. The unbeliever is a rational and mortal nature who willingly flees from life and thinks that his own Creator, who exists forever, does not exist. 5. The lawless man is he who holds the law of God with his own wickedness and with contrary heresy, and supposes that he believes in God. 6. A Christian is an imitation of Christ, as far as is humanly possible, and one who in deed, word and mind believes rightly and blamelessly in the Holy Trinity. 7. The lover of God is he who keeps natural and sinless deeds unalterably, and who is not negligent in any good that is possible for him. 8. The continent man is he who, amid temptations, snares and tumults, strives to accomplish the deeds of those who are removed from all such things. 9. Monasticism is the rule and work of the bodiless ones, accomplished in material and mortal flesh. 10. A monk is he who does and beholds only what is God's, at every time, in every place and in every deed.
11. Monasticism is this: that a person abandons his own will, gathers together all his scattered thoughts, and is watchful in everything.

12. Monasticism is a perpetual forcing of nature and an unfailing guarding of the senses. 13. Monasticism is an undefiled body, a pure mouth, and a mind enlightened and seeing. 14. A monk is a sorrowing soul, afflicted by the perpetual remembrance of death, whether he is asleep or awake.

15. Separation from and renunciation of nature, out of desire for those good things that are above nature. 16. All who have abandoned the affairs of the world have done so either because of the multitude of their sins, or for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, or for love of God. But if not one of these three thoughts has become their guide, their departure is brutish; yet in every case our good King awaits the end of the matter, to see what it will be. 17. Let him who has gone out from the world to scatter the burden of his sins liken himself to those who sit by the tombs outside the city, and let him not cease from hot, fire-like, blazing tears and from the hidden lamentations of the heart, until he too sees Jesus come to him, so that the stone of hard-heartedness from his heart
he may roll away, and may loose his bound mind, like Lazarus, from the bonds [?] of sin;
when he commands his angels: "Loose him from the passions and let him go on the way of blessed passionlessness."
But if it does not happen in this way, his departure from the world will be of no profit to him. As many of us as wish to go out from Egypt and to flee from the bitter slavery of Pharaoh,
we too undoubtedly need some Moses as a mediator with God, that he may stand for us between action and contemplation;
and may stretch out his hands to God, so that those who follow him may cross the sea of sins and may become victorious over the Amalek of the passions,
for all those are mistaken who give themselves over to such battles and think that they have no need of a guide.
19. Those who [?] as their guide, while those who came out from Sodom [had] an angel. And now too those who the healing of the passions of the soul [?]
seek, they are like those who came out of Egypt, who need a physician like Moses;
but those who desire to strip off this wretched flesh of impurity need an angel, that is, one equal to an angel, if I may put it so,
as a helper, for according to the greatness and festering of the wounds we also need a skilled physician. Truly great hardship and unceasing labor are needed
by those who have undertaken to ascend to heaven with the flesh, and especially at the start and beginning of their departure from the world,
until that pleasure-loving habit of ours and that merciless heart come, through mourning, to the love of God and to purity.
For truly great labor and much bitterness are required, and especially for those of us who have become accustomed to the passions,
until we make this mind of ours, which like a dog loves the flesh and loves [?], into a lover of purity and a lover of wisdom, through meekness, steadfastness, and freedom from anger.
Yet let us who are subject to passions and weak not be without hope, but with unwavering faith our weakness and the feebleness of our soul,
let us hold out to Christ with our right hand and confess them, and without doubt we shall receive from him help beyond our worthiness,
if only we continually bring ourselves down into the abyss of humility. 21. Know
that those who approach the fierce and narrow, yet light, contest have come to enter a fire, since they expect to receive that immaterial fire within themselves.
Let each one test himself, and so let him [?] of that fruit, the [?] of the field mixed with tears,
so that his soldiering may not be to his own condemnation. If not everyone who has been baptized is saved, I shall pass over in silence what follows from this. All who wish to become monks,
let them leave behind every affair of the world, and let them despise everything, and let them renounce everything when they come to become monks,
so that they may lay a good foundation. The good foundation consists of the three pillars of virtue: innocence, fasting, and purity. And let all who are infants in Christ
make their beginning with these deeds, and let them take visible infants as their model, for nowhere is craftiness or crookedness found among them,
nor insatiable gorging, nor an unfillable belly, nor inflamed or bestial flesh; but, as I suppose,
as their nourishment increases, they also take on heat. Truly hateful and ruinous it is when a soldier goes into battle
and immediately upon entering grows slack and gives to all an image of his own death, for when others see

that he went in and was killed, they no longer wish to enter that battle. Without doubt, if we enter upon monastic life well and vigorously from the very beginning of our labors, it will be of great benefit
to us, if after some time we do not grow slack;
for a soul that has been emboldened and then grows slack again is pricked, as if by a spur, by the remembrance of its former zeal.
For this reason, many times, by this means, many have given wings to themselves, for they were like eagles whose wings had fallen;
and afterward they recovered their wings and rose to the height of heaven. When the soul betrays itself and loses that blessed and longed-for ardor of its own,
let him diligently investigate for what cause he lost it, and let him direct all his diligence toward that,
for it is not possible for it to return by any other door than the one by which it went out. He whose going out from the world,
often resembles incense thrown into the fire, which at first begins as fragrance and in the end turns to smoke.
But he who goes out in order to receive a reward is a mill ground by a donkey, which goes round continually when it sees its reward, and continually turns along one path.
But he whose separation is for the love of God, immediately, with his very going out,
has acquired that blessed fire; and when that fire has entered into fuel, the further it advances,
the higher it will kindle its flame. There are those who build [?]; and there are others who erect pillars on sand;
and there are others who, having run a little on their feet and their sinews and joints having been loosened, afterward run faster.
Let him who understands understand this word of parable. As those called by God and the King, let us run with zeal,
lest, our life in this world being but a short time, we be found fruitless on the day of death and perish of hunger. Let us be pleasing to the Lord,
as soldiers are to the king, for after we have entered military service, faithful service to him is required of us. Let us fear the Lord as we fear wild beasts;
for I have seen men who went out to steal and had no fear of God, but when they heard the sound of dogs in that place,
they became afraid and immediately turned back; what the fear of God could not do with them, the fear of dogs did.
Let us love the Lord as we love friends in the flesh, for I have seen men who angered God and had no concern about it at all;
and again I have seen those same men, when they had embittered their friends over some small matter, seek every means and try every way,
and show every sorrow, and make every apology, by themselves and through friends and through relatives, and with gifts and bribes,
in order to bring that friend back to the former state. At the beginning of our going out from the world, we undoubtedly practice the virtues with labor and hardship and bitterness;
and when we have advanced in them, we may afterward be without distress, or with only a little sorrow and labor;
but when our mortal nature is swallowed up and mastered by zeal,
then let us practice them with all diligence and joy and desire and divine flame. As praiseworthy as are those who from the very beginning fulfill the commandments with all joy and zeal,
so pitiable are those who have spent a long time in the monastic life and still do this with labor, even if they do it. Nor
let us despise a going out from the world [of this kind], for I have seen certain fugitives who unwillingly came upon the king and met him,

and afterward willingly went along with him, came to the palace, and sat down at table with him. I have seen seed that fell to the ground unintentionally, and it sprouted and spread and produced much fruit;
and other seed was sown deliberately, and it proved fruitless.
I have seen someone who came to a place of healing for some other need, and he was seized by the physician's eagerness and was healed, and the dimness spread over his eyes was stripped away,

and these things that happen involuntarily are many times firmer and truer than some voluntary ones. Let no one plead the weight and multitude of his sins as an excuse, saying of himself that he is unworthy of the monastic way of life,
and, out of love of pleasure, imagine that he is humbling himself, and make excuses with the excuse of sin;
for where the wound is great, there great healing is also needed, so that the venom may be cleansed away, for it is not the healthy
but the sick who come to be healed. If an earthly king had called us to serve him before his face,
we would not keep him waiting, we would not make excuses, but we would leave everything behind and hurry there.
So let us take care for ourselves against holding back [?] from the King of kings, and Lord of lords, and God of gods, who calls us to the heavenly order;
let us not treat him with contempt, and let us not separate ourselves from him through our negligence and laziness, so that we may not be found speechless and ashamed before that great throne.

It is possible even for one bound by the affairs of the world, fettered with the fetters of cares, to walk, but only with difficulty, for those who have fetters on their feet also walk, but they fall again and again, and wounds come upon them from this. Whoever is unmarried in the world and bound only by its affairs is like a man whose hands alone are bound; therefore, when he wishes to run on the path of monasticism, he is not prevented. But whoever is married is like one bound hand and foot. I heard some people who were living negligently in the world, who said to me: "How can we, who are joined to spouses and are in the service of royal affairs, enter the monastic life?" And I answered and said to them: "Do all the good that you are able: slander no one, steal nothing, lie to no one, exalt yourselves over no one, hate no one, do not be absent from church, have mercy on the poor, cause no one to stumble; do not seize another's share, and do not touch a stranger's body, and let your spouses be enough for you.
If you do all this, you are not far from the kingdom of heaven." Let us approach that contest, and let us not be afraid of our enemies, for they closely observe the face of our soul, even though

[...] they cannot see; and if they see the face of the soul changed by fear, then they arm themselves more bitterly against us, for those crafty ones perceive that we have become afraid. Let us arm ourselves bravely against them, for no one makes war on one who fights zealously. By his providence the Lord has lightened the battles for those newly come, so that they may not return to the world immediately, at the very beginning. Therefore rejoice in the Lord always, all you servants of the Lord, and take this first as a sign of the love that the King has for you, and be fully assured that he has called you. God also often does this: when he sees brave souls, he lets battles loose on them at the very beginning, so that he may quickly crown them. The Lord has hidden from lay people the difficulty, or rather the ease, of this racecourse; for if all knew it, not many would become monks. Give the labors of your youth zealously to the Lord, and in your old age you will rejoice over the wealth of dispassion. Labors gathered in youth nourish and console those who have grown weak in old age. Let us labor fervently, you young men, let us run well, for the hour of death is unknown. Truly we have evil and wicked enemies, crafty and full of many devices, sleepless and cunning, bodiless and invisible, who have fire in their hands and strive to burn the temple of God with their flame. Let no young man accept the counsel of the enemies when they say to him: "Do not crush and waste your flesh in this way, lest you

fall into diseases and infirmities." For in this generation scarcely anyone can be found who would wish to put his flesh entirely to death, even if he were only to keep himself from many and tasty foods.
But [?] of that devil who would urge such counsel [?].
This is his intent: that the beginning and entry should be slackened by the warfare, and that the end should then be made like the beginning.
Above all, let those who wish to serve the Lord well seek this: that by the counsel and very careful discernment of spiritual fathers they should acquire places, occupations and rules of life such
as would suit each one's life; for communities are not good for everyone, because of gluttony, nor are places of solitary stillness better for everyone, because of anger,
but let each one understand by which he is overcome. The whole monastic life is comprised in three forms of settled living:
either to live apart and struggle in solitude, or to live in stillness with one or two others, or to remain patiently in a community. Solomon says in Ecclesiastes:
"But walk on the royal road," for the middle of those previously mentioned is suitable for many. Of the one it is said,
that when he [?] into despondency, or sleep, or laxity, or [?] (Ecclesiastes 4:10) and he has no one to raise him up.
But the Lord says (Matthew 18:20). Who then is that wise and faithful and blessed monk who has kept his fervor unquenched
until the day of his departure from the body, and who every day has not ceased adding fire to fire, longing to longing, fervor to fervor,
and zeal to zeal, until he comes before the Lord pure and spotless? To him belongs glory, now and always and forever and ever.
Amen. The first ascent of the ladder of virtues; whoever has completed this, let him not turn back perversely from it.

Said by the same blessed father of ours, John. On hatred of the world and of its possessions. Chapter 2. Whoever truly comes to love the Lord, and whoever truly seeks to attain that eternal kingdom, and whoever truly acquires pain for his own sins, whoever truly acquires the remembrance of torment and eternal punishment, and whoever truly establishes in his heart the fear of his departure from the body, will no longer love, nor take care, nor be anxious about necessities, or possessions, or kin, or the glory of the world; or friends, or brothers, or anything at all among the affairs of the earth. Instead, he will cast away and hate all love and all care for all this, and before all this, his own flesh, and naked and carefree and with courage he will follow Christ, and will look always to heaven, and await help from him, according to the word of the holy one: "[?] mine after you, and your right hand has received me," who, that blessed one, said:

2. It is a great shame if, having left behind all that was mentioned before, and after that calling with which the Lord called us, and not a man, we should care about some matter that would not be able to do any good
to us at the time of our distress, which is death. For this is why the Lord said: 3. The Lord knew how quickly we turn aside from the good way of life, we who have newly come out of the world;
and that, if we associate with lay people, we easily turn back to the world again. For this reason he said to the one who asked, "Let me go and bury my father,"
And the Lord said to him: [?] 4. After our departure from the world, the demons persuade us to call merciful and compassionate lay people blessed, and to blame ourselves,
as though we have stripped ourselves of all their virtue. But this is the intent of our enemies, that by that vain and untrue humility
they may either turn us back to the world, or, even if we remain in monastic life, cast us into despair.
5. There is a contempt of lay people out of pride, and there is again a contempt of them
when they do not hear, for the sake of fleeing from despair and acquiring hope. Let us hear what the Lord says to that young man,
who said that he had kept all the commandments: "Go, sell all your possessions and give to the poor, and become poor, and receive charity from others." Of whom [?]
[?] going, let us wisely understand that the Lord called even those living in the world, though alive, dead,
and he said to someone: "Leave the dead, the lay people, that they may bury those dead in the flesh who are among them."
8. That wealth did not in any way hinder that young man from baptism, and therefore some have surely erred who said that the Lord spoke to him about coming to baptism,
saying, "Sell your possessions." And such assurance as this is enough to convince us of the great glory of this way of life of ours.
9. It is to be examined why those who were engaged in vigils, fasting, and labor, when they come to become monks and withdraw from the world,
And when they come to the testing of their deeds, they are unable to carry on that former false and [?] vain striving of theirs.
10. I have seen many and various plants of the virtues, planted by those living in the world,
and they were watered as if from a channel of filth, and were dug around by vainglory and ostentation,
and that dung of [?] was poured [?] on their roots. And when they were transplanted to a land [?] trodden and traveled by lay people and [?] watered by that water of vainglory and stench,
they immediately withered, for plants accustomed to such watering do not thrive in the harsh and waterless land that is the testing ground of true ascetic striving.

11. Whoever has willingly hated the world has been delivered from sorrows; but whoever has love for any visible thing has not yet been freed from sorrow, for how could he not be grieved at the loss of what he loves? 12. In all things great caution is needed by us, but above all let us guard, with a careful mind, against what I intend to speak of. 13. Many, through the cares and anxieties and labors and vigils of bodily life, have escaped the burning and raging of their bodies; but when such people come to the monastic life and become free of care, the wretched ones are defiled by the arousal of the body. 14. Let us guard ourselves, lest we suppose that we are walking the narrow and hard way when we are holding to the wide and broad way and going astray. 15. This is the narrow way: constraint [?] of the belly; standing all night in psalmody; drinking water by measure; going short of bread; enduring shame and reproach; accepting mockery and contempt; cutting off one's own wills; not murmuring at insult; patience in hardships; submitting to abuse; bearing the sight of evils [?]; not growing angry at contempt; and if anyone seizes what is ours, let us forgive it without a word;
and if anyone speaks evil to us, let us not be distressed but bear it with patience; let us forgive and not seek repayment; or if any judge us, let us humble ourselves before them

without a word. And this is the narrow way of the monastic life. 16. Blessed are those who walk on this way of the works spoken of above, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. 17. No one will enter the heavenly bridal chamber crowned unless he has achieved the first and second and third separation: that is, first from the world and possessions and kin; second from his own will; and the third separation from vainglory, and separation from it produces obedience. 18. For who among those of the world has ever performed miracles, who has raised the dead, who has driven out demons? No one. For all these are the works of monks, which the world cannot contain and is not capable of; for if it were capable of them, separation and the monastic life would be useless and superfluous. 19. When the demons, after our departure, inflame our hearts with the remembrance of our parents and brothers,

Then let us arm ourselves with prayer against them, and let us warm ourselves with the remembrance of that eternal fire, so that by remembering it we may quench the improper fire of our heart and kindle the divine fire among us. 20. Whoever thinks that he has despised something, and then becomes grieved over its loss, such a person is wholly deceiving himself. 21. All young men who are inclined to carnal love and pleasure, and who wish to come to the monastic life,

let them take care with all diligence and remove themselves from every pleasure and wickedness, so that their last state may not become worse than their first. A harbor can become a place of captivity, and all who travel on the visible sea and all who travel on the invisible sea know this. This is a pitiable thing, when those who have escaped from the heart of the sea are sunk within the harbor. This is the second step of the Ladder of virtues, on which you have set your foot: imitate not the wife, but Lot in his flight.

On Exile. Chapter 3. Exile: [?] parents and all those in our land who oppose and hinder that good intention of ours. This exile is separation from boldness, unknown wisdom, unrevealed knowledge, a hidden life, an unseen understanding,

an invisible thought, a desire for shame and reproach, a longing for hardship and affliction, a growth of divine desire, a multiplication of the love of God, a renunciation of arrogance, an abyss of silence. This resolve too, which is separation from one's own people, often at the beginning, through that fire which is from God, powerfully compels the lovers of God out of desire for hardships and sorrows. But however great and desirable this thing is, it requires just as much discernment and understanding, for not all exile is good. If every prophet is held in contempt in his own city and homeland, according to the word of the Lord, then let us also take care that exile does not become for us something that increases vainglory.

Exile has made the mind inseparable from God. True exile is the love and practice of unforgetting mourning. Exile [?], and let one flee from love of strangers as well. When you are going forth to the monastic life or to exile, do not wait for world-loving souls, for that thief, which is death, is impatient and grants no delay. Many wished to save the negligent,
and they too perished with them, when over a length of time that fire was quenched from their soul and the heat grew cold. Having received the divine flame, run,
for you do not know when it may be quenched and leave you in darkness. Not all of us will be judged concerning others, as to why we did not save them,
but concerning ourselves all without doubt will be judged, for the Apostle says that [?], and again he says: [?]
While you are in exile, beware of the devil of wandering about and of love of pleasure, for exile gives him occasion. It is good to despise possessions,
but its mother is exile.

Let everyone who becomes a stranger for the Lord's sake no longer acquire any carnal and unprofitable love, whether for possessions or for a person, so that his occupation may not be wandering about for the sake of the passions rather than exile. Let him who has become a stranger to the world no longer touch the world, for the passions love to return. Eve was driven out of paradise against her will,
and the monk goes out willingly from his fatherland and his own country,
for she again felt desire for that tree of disobedience, while this one suffered harm every day from kinsfolk and friends. Flee as from fire from the places of your fall, where sin has befallen you,
for when we do not see those fruits of bitterness anywhere, we do not constantly desire them. Do not be ignorant of this device and craftiness of those evil rulers,
for they urge us not to separate ourselves from lay people, as though a great reward would be given to us

if we look at women and let loose the bridle on ourselves, yet they do not lead us astray; but let us rather do the opposite. When we have separated ourselves from our own people for some time and have acquired some small compunction or reverence,

then those vain thoughts of vainglory come upon us and tell us to return again to our own country, for the benefit of many, as an example of good, and for the edification of those who knew of our evil deeds and were caused to stumble by them,
and if we have some word of teaching or some small understanding, then, as
saviors of our souls, they urge us to return to the world, so that what we have gathered well in the harbor we may wretchedly scatter in the heart of the sea. Let us not be like Lot's wife,
but let us be like Lot in flight, for the soul that returns to the place from which it went out melts like salt
and becomes an immovable monument. Flee [?]; those who turned back again to Egypt did not see that land of dispassion [?], Jerusalem. This too happens,

for when certain tender beginners have gone out from their own country and have been completely purified, it is good for them to return there again with this thought: that after their own salvation they may save others too,
for Moses too, that seer of God, was sent by God to lead out his own people; he had many kinsfolk in Egypt,
which is darkness. It is better to grieve parents than the Lord, for he created us and saved us,

while they have many times destroyed those they loved and given them over to torment. That is true exile, when one sits among foreign tongues without a tongue, in understanding. Is it out of hatred for our own people and our countries that we go away from them? Far from it! But from them

comes harm upon us as well, and we go on account of ruin from our ascetic struggle. Just as Christ became a pattern for us in every good thing, so too in this, for he too many times left his fleshly kinsfolk; and for this reason, when they once said to him: [?]
And at once that good teacher and our Lord showed a dispassionate hatred and said to them,
that: Let your father be he who labors together with you in the bearing of your sins, and helps you, and strengthens you;

And let your mother be compunction and weeping, which are able to wash you clean of the stains of your sins; and let your brother be one who labors and runs with you in the race on the road that leads up to heaven. Acquire as your inseparable spouse the remembrance of death; and let your beloved children be the sighs of the heart; and acquire your flesh as a slave.
And as friends, those holy powers who are able to be of great benefit to you at the time of death,

if they become your friends. Longing for God extinguishes longing for parents, and whoever says, "I am able to hold on to both," deceives himself, for he does not understand what God says, that no one is able [?]. The Lord says that father and mothers against children, and

brothers against brothers, those who wish to serve me: enmity and separation of the lovers of God from the lovers of the world, of the material from the immaterial, and of the lovers of glory from the humble. For the Lord rejoices at a separation that comes about for the sake of love of him. See,
see and take care, lest, when the whole world is being filled with water, you become a lover of the company of your relatives and parents,

and do not enter that ark of ascetic struggle, and perish in that flood of love of the world. Do not pity the tears of parents or friends, lest you weep forever. When your relatives surround you like bees, or rather like wasps, and make lament over you,
then firmly and unbendingly direct the eyes of your soul toward your deeds and your death, so that by pain you may be able to drive pain out of you. Those who are not our own proclaim to us,

saying: "We will do everything just as you wish and whatever you love." But this is their inner thought: that they might ruin that good race of ours, and then by some contrivance lead us to their own will. Let our departure from our country be to places

that are harsh, where no bodily consolation is to be found, and where vainglory does not come to us, but rather humiliation; but if we do not do so, we are flying on the wings of the passions. Flee from revealing that you are the child of rulers and of your noble rank, lest you be found saying one thing with your mouth and showing another by your deeds. No one has given himself to exile so unwaveringly as that great man who heard, that he who [?] was being called to a foreign tongue and a land of barbarians. This too often happens,
that the Lord glorifies, in the likeness of that great Abraham, one who has gone out into exile for the sake of his name;
but even if that glory is given by God, it is nevertheless good to turn it away with the shield of humility. When demons,
as if for some great virtue, praise us, or even men, on account of our exile, then let us remember that One who came from heaven to earth,
and became a stranger for our sake, and let us find ourselves,

that even if we were to struggle for [?] ages and become strangers, we cannot repay him in equal measure. Grievous and exceedingly evil is fleshly love, whether toward one's relatives or toward some stranger, for it is able to turn us back to the world and entirely extinguish that fire of our compunction, if we give it room.
M [?]. Just as it is impossible to look toward heaven with one eye and toward the earth with the other, so likewise it is impossible
for a soul not to be harmed if it has not become entirely estranged from its own people, in mind or also in body. Through much labor and diligence good habit makes progress in us,
and what has progressed through the labor of many years can be lost in the moment of a single hour; for sweet minds and good customs are corrupted by
evil thoughts and the shameful things of the world. Whoever, after leaving the world, still keeps company with the world or stays close to it will without doubt either fall into the same snares
into which he had fallen before, or his heart will be defiled by seeing and hearing them; or, if he is not defiled himself, he will judge those who are defiled, and in this way he will be defiled.
On dreams. The mind of our understanding is worthless and full of every lack of understanding, and this cannot be hidden;
for the palate distinguishes foods, and the [ears? the text has "drinks"] recognize the sense of words; for the sun reveals the weakness of the eyes,
but words reveal the lack of understanding of the soul. Yet love compels a person according to his ability. And therefore I shall speak as I understand,

for I suppose, though I do not determine or affirm it, that after we depart into exile dreams make war on us. For this reason I wished, in the chapter on exile, to say a little about dreams as well, so that we may not be ignorant of this device also of those crafty enemies of ours.
A dream is a movement of the mind while the body is motionless. Fantasy is a deception of the eyes in the sleeping mind. Fantasy is an astonishment of the mind

while the body is awake. Fantasy is a vision that is bodiless and has no existence. The reason why I wished to speak about dreams in the chapter on exile is plainly evident. When for the Lord's sake we have left our homes and kin and others of ours,
and have given ourselves over to exile for the love of God,
then the demons trouble us through dreams and show us our own people as if mourning,

or as if dying, or as imprisoned and afflicted on our account. Whoever trusts dreams is like the man who chases his own shadow and wishes to catch it. The demons of vainglory become prophets in sleep, for they bring us tidings of future events; yet they know nothing of the things to come, but either they lie, or the event has already occurred and they have learned of it by some other means, or they have heard something about it in another place, or have seen it, and have learned it as if by devices, and they come quickly and tell us, and even that by conjecture. If their word comes to pass, they rejoice; and if it does not come to pass, they do not grieve. When the dreams we have seen come to pass, we are amazed, as though we had drawn near to the grace of foreknowledge, and we become greatly puffed up.
To those who trust the devil he often becomes a prophet, but to those who despise him he always appears a liar. He is a spirit, and he sees the things done within this air,
and he learns of the death of someone dying, and goes and tells the foolish, and appears among them as a prophet. They know nothing of future events by foreknowledge,
Otherwise sorcerers too would be able to foretell death. They often transform themselves into angels of light and into the form of martyrs,
and they show us in sleep as if we were going to them, and when we wake they fill us with joy and conceit. Let this be the sign of their deception,
for true angels show us torments and judgments and the separation of the soul from the body, and when we wake, trembling,
we become frightened and sorrowful. When we begin to trust the demons in sleep, then they mock us even when we are awake. He who believes in dreams
is altogether inexperienced,
but he who does not believe them at all is all-wise. All those who show us judgment and torments,
believe them;
but if despair fights against you, that too comes from the demons.
The third step of the ladder of virtues, by the power of the Holy Trinity. You who have completed it upon this holy [?], no longer look to the right or to the left.
Discourse of our holy and blessed father John. Chapter 4. On all-praised and beautiful obedience. 1. Our discourse has in its due time arrived at those zealous ones and strivers of Christ,
for before all fruit goes the flower, and before all obedience goes exile, whether of the body or of the will, without doubt; for by these two virtues,
as by two golden wings, blessed obedience ascends to heaven without hindrance;

and perhaps it was of this that the prophet clothed with the Spirit spoke when he sang: by deed, by contemplation and by humility. Let us not fail to set forth the image of those brave horsemen, to make known by our discourse how they hold the shield of faith in God and in their own teacher, and by it turn aside every thought of unbelief or of moving elsewhere;
and they draw the sword of the Spirit, and cut down all their own will;

and they are clothed with the chain mail of meekness and patience, and stand unwounded by all the arrows of insult and contempt; and they have the helmet of salvation, which is the protection of the teacher's prayers; and as for their feet, they do not merely stand with them joined together, but one toward service
they have stretched out, and the other they hold unmoved from prayer. Obedience is the renunciation of one's own soul, shown completely and openly through the body; or else thus:
obedience is the killing of the members with a living mind. Obedience is unquestioning movement and voluntary death, an unexamined life, carefree hardship, an unrehearsed giving of account to God.

It is fearlessness of death, a voyage on the sea without sinking, and a journey made in sleep. Obedience is the grave of the will and the resurrection of humility. The man dead through obedience does not answer back,
nor does he distinguish the good from the things that seem to him to be evil,
for he who has put his own soul to death in the fear of God,

he will give account for it. Obedience is parting from the riches of wisdom and understanding, while in wealth of them. The beginning of the killing both of the members of the body and of the wills of the soul
is hardship and pain, the middle is sometimes pain and sometimes freedom from pain, and the end is complete freedom from pain, unawareness of pain.

Only then is that living and blessed dead man pained and burned, when he sees himself carrying out his own will, for he is afraid of bearing his own judgment. All you who are prepared to enter this arena of spiritual martyrdom,
as many of you as wish to bear the yoke of the Lord on your necks, as many as hasten beforehand to lay your own burden on the shoulders of another; you who willingly
desire to write a bond of slavery in your own hand, and in exchange wish to have freedom written for yourselves,

as many as, lifted up on the hands of others, are crossing over this great sea: know, you who are such, that you have begun to travel a short and harsh road, on which there is no error except one, which is called self-rule.
But whoever utterly renounces this, and does not do his own will even in whatever seems to him good and spiritual, has arrived before setting out,
for obedience is distrust of oneself in everything,
until the end of life. When we are zealous for the Lord's sake to bend our necks, with the thought of humility and of the divine life, then before our entry, if there is any wisdom in us

and sharpness of mind, let us search and examine, and, that I may say this also, let us test the guide with whom we are entering, so that we may not come to a sailor as to a master of sailors, to a sick man
as to a physician, to one subject to passions as to one free of passions, and enter the heart of the sea as if it were a harbor,

and soon meet with drowning. But after entering the arena of the service of God and of obedience, let us no longer judge our teacher and the guide of our good in anything at all, even if we see some deficiency in him,
as in a man. Otherwise, if we judge him in anything, know that we will gain no profit from obedience. It is fitting for those who wish always to keep toward their guides
an unwavering faith that they should keep their virtues in their hearts indelibly and as an everlasting remembrance,
so that when the demons send unbelief upon them, they may turn them back by the remembrance of those good deeds; for as much as faith increases in the heart,

so much also is the body vigorous and eager in service. But when it has stumbled through unbelief, it falls, as the Apostle says. When the thought comes upon you to judge your teacher, flee from it as from fornication,
and give no place at all to this serpent, but answer that dragon and say to him: O deceiver,
it is not I who am the judge of that superior, but he who is judge of me,

for it is not I who have borne his burden, but he who has borne mine. The holy ones [?] and prayer as a wall, and those spotless tears as a bath. And they proclaimed blessed obedience a martyrdom, and without it no one of those entangled in sins and passions shall see the face of the Lord.
He who passes sentence on himself.
For if he submits completely for God's sake,

Even though it may seem to him that he has not taken off his burden, in fact he has cast it away entirely. But if he carries out his own will in certain matters, then even though he may think he has taken off his burden, he is still carrying it himself. This is all the more so if his teacher does not refrain from rebuking him. But if the teacher does refrain and leaves him unrebuked, I do not know what to say about this. Those who by [?],
walk on a good road, for they do not, by scheming and close scrutiny, stir up the machinations of the devil against themselves.
First of all, let us confess our sins to our good superior alone; and if he commands us, let us confess them before everyone as well,
for wounds, the more they are shown, do not grow hard but are healed. I once came to a monastery, and there I saw a terrible judgment of the good judge and shepherd.
For while I was there, a man from a band of robbers came to become a monk.
And that good shepherd and physician ordered that he be given complete rest for seven days, so that he might simply observe the rule of the monastery.
After that week the shepherd called him to himself and asked him whether it pleased him to stay with them.
And when he saw that the man promised this wholeheartedly, he asked him again about the deeds he had done in the world, and he saw that he confessed them eagerly and fervently.
Then, to test him, he said to him again: "I want you to confess all these sins of yours before all the brothers." But the man truly hated his sins and despised all shame,
and so he promised to do this without hesitation, and said: "If you wish, I will tell them even in the city of Alexandria."
Then the shepherd gathered in the church all those rational sheep, two hundred and thirty in number.

And while the holy man was celebrating the liturgy, for that day was Sunday, after the reading of the Gospel he brought in that reproached yet blameless man. Several brothers were dragging him and beating him lightly;
his hands were bound behind him, he was clothed in sackcloth of [?], and on his head
ashes had been sprinkled, so that at the mere sight everyone was astonished and lamented with weeping, for no one knew what he intended to do. And when he drew near the doors of the church,
that blessed and holy father called out in a loud voice and said: "Stand there, for you are not worthy to enter here."
And he was startled at the voice of the shepherd when he heard it from the sanctuary; for, as he himself afterward assured us with an oath:
"I thought it was the sound of thunder and not the voice of a man." And he immediately fell on his face, trembling and distressed with fear,
and lying on the ground he drenched the place with tears. And that wonderful physician again gave him a command,

he who in all things sought his salvation and made him a mirror of salvation and an image of true humility: he then told him to tell his deeds before everyone. And he confessed with trembling, one by one, all his astonishing deeds,
not only those that were carnal and according to nature, but also those contrary to nature,
and sorceries and murders, and other things that it is not fitting to hear;
And after the confession, he ordered that he be tonsured and numbered among the brothers. But I marveled at the wisdom of that holy man, and I asked him why he had done that strange thing.
And that true physician answered and said to me: I did this for two reasons. First, so that by this shame I might deliver him from the eternal shame,
and so it came about, for he had not yet risen from the ground, Brother John, before he had found forgiveness of everything.
Or will you be unbelieving about this? For one of the brothers standing there told me: I saw a certain terrible man who had paper and writing in his hands, and a pen,
and as the man lying prostrate spoke his sins, he too drew the pen across that paper and blotted them out; and rightly so, for it is written:
And secondly I did this because there are some here who have unconfessed sins, and I showed them this as an example, so that they too may come to confession,
for without confession no one attains forgiveness of sins. And I saw many other wondrous and memorable deeds with that shepherd and flock, most of which I will hasten to make known to you.
For I stayed there no small time and examined their way of life, and I marveled at how those of earth had been made like those of heaven.
For they were bound with the bond of love, indissolubly, and this is the wonderful thing: they were separated from all boldness and idle talk, and their struggle before all else was for this,
that they should not wound the mind of a brother in anything at all,
and if anyone showed himself a hater of his brother, that shepherd would send such a one away to the separate monastery,

as one to be punished, for there was a separate monastery for those who had sinned. And once a certain brother spoke evil of a brother in his presence, and immediately that holy man ordered him to be driven out altogether, saying that it is not right that there should be

in the monastery both a visible and an invisible devil. I saw among those saints astonishing deeds full of profit, a God-gathered assembly bound together by love, whose deeds and appearance alike were wonderful, for they so trained and shepherded themselves in the virtues
that they did not even need the reproof of the superior, but of their own accord they roused one another toward those divine works,
for they had divine rules and works established and firmly fixed. And if the superior was not there,
and someone began slander, or judging, or idle talk, another would secretly alert him with a sign and make him stop,
and if he did not notice,

or did not listen, the one who had made the sign would immediately rise, bend his knees in a prostration, and go away. And unforgettable among them, and I would say unceasing, was the thought and complete remembrance of death, and talk of the eternal punishment. I will not keep silent in telling you about the deed of their cook,
for when I saw that he had unchanging sorrow and constant tears in his service, I begged him to tell me how he had been made worthy of such grace;
But when I pressed him, he said to me: "I have never thought that I am serving men, but God; and of all stillness
I have considered myself unworthy; and I keep this sight of this fire as a reminder of that eternal fire." Let us hear another wondrous virtue of theirs,
for not even at table did they rest from spiritual works and contemplations, but by an established
hidden sign, by making a signal, those blessed ones reminded one another of spiritual prayer; and they did this not only at table,

but at every meeting and gathering. And if anyone committed some fault, the others would earnestly beg him to allow them to speak on his behalf to the abbot, and to take upon themselves the canonical penance and punishment for it.
The abbot knew this too, and for this reason he would give such men a light penance,
and would no longer seek out the one who had truly committed the fault. Where among them was any matter of idle speech or insolence to be found?
And if someone began a quarrel with his neighbor, a second brother would come and fall down before him on bended knee,

and would dispel that anger. But if he saw him still persisting in rancor, he would report it to the second after the abbot, and that one would thus strive that they be reconciled with one another before sunset.
If he again saw him still hardened, he would either impose abstinence from food until they were reconciled with one another, or expel him from the monastery.
And it was not in vain that this was observed and that they practiced such fine strictness; rather, it brought forth much fruit,
and it showed this among them. For many of those saints proved to be ascetic strugglers, knowers of hidden things, discerning and humble.
And an awesome and angelic sight was to be seen among them, for old men and elders ran to obedience like tender children,
and they held humility as their great boast. I saw men there who had spent more than fifty years in obedience,
whom I begged to tell me what fruit they had gained from so much labor, and some of whom
told me that they had reached the abyss of humility, by which they turn back every assault,
and others said that they possessed complete insensibility and freedom from pain amid insults and contempt. I saw others of good report among those beasts [?] who were likened to angels,
having reached the depth of simplicity and innocence, acquired through wisdom, voluntary and advanced in God, not anything brutish and senseless, like those mad old men of the world,
whom people call mad; rather, they were outwardly sweet, radiant, and kind, and their speech and manner were not contrived and crooked, but plain and cheerful.
This is not found among many. But inwardly, in spirit, their scent toward God and toward their superior was like that of innocent children,
and the eyes of their minds were watchful and firm against demons and passions. The time of my life does not suffice me, O holy father and God-loving assembly, to recount the virtue
and the angel-like life of those blessed ones; but it is good that we should adorn this discourse of ours to you with their sweat and labors, and rouse you to zeal for the love of God,
rather than with our own words and teachings, for undoubtedly the lesser is adorned by the greater.
But this I beseech of you: let no one imagine that anything written by us is a lie, for little faith is accustomed to corrupt what is profitable.
But now let us return to our first discourse. There was a certain man named Isidore, one of the rulers of the city of Alexandria, and a monk

he became in the aforementioned monastery, which I too reached there. That holy shepherd received him, and saw him to be vehement and negligent, haughty and boastful; and the blessed one, with human skill, devised a stratagem against the machinations of the demons, and said to Isidore:
"If you wish to take the yoke of Christ upon your neck, I want you before all else to acquire obedience."
And he said to him: "As iron obeys the smith, so have I given myself over in obedience to you, O holy one of God." And the blessed man was pleased with the figure he had spoken,
and immediately gave a task of testing to that iron-like Isidore, and said: "It is my wish, brother, that you stand at the gates of the monastery,
and bend your knees to all who come in and go out, and say to them: 'Pray for me, fathers, for I am mad and full of gall.'" And he obeyed him,
as an angel of the Lord is obedient. And when he had spent seven years in that work, and had attained the depth of humility and compunction, the blessed man wished, after that period of seven years,
and because of his mighty endurance, to number him with the brethren and make him worthy of the blessing.
But he put forward many others, and me too, the feeble one, to entreat the shepherd to allow him to remain in that same work and to finish his course.
And by a hint in his words he indicated his departure from this world and the end of his life, and so it came to pass. Then the abbot left him in that same work,
and after ten days he passed to the Lord, from dishonor to glory,
and on the seventh day after

his death the doorkeeper of the monastery was also taken away by the Lord, for that blessed man had promised him: "If I find boldness before the Lord, you shall not be parted from me in that age to come, and I will soon take you away."
And so he did, as a sign of his unashamed obedience
and his Christ-like humility. I asked that great Isidore, while he was still with us, what occupation held his mind

as he sat at the gates of the monastery, and that man of good memory did not conceal what was profitable, but said to me: "At the beginning I trained myself in this thought: that I had been sold on account of my sins,
and therefore with hardship and labor and blood I performed the bending of the knees. And when one year had been completed, my heart was untroubled,
and I awaited from God the reward of my labor and obedience. And when one year had been completed,
I had something else established in my heart: that I am not worthy to be in the monastery, or to see and converse with the fathers, or to receive the holy mysteries, or to look upon anyone's face,

And for this reason I made prostrations in this way to those coming in and going out, and my eyes looked at the ground, and my mind increased in humility, and with a fervent heart I asked everyone for prayer. One day I sat at table with this great teacher;
and he brought his holy mouth close to my ear and said to me: "Do you wish me to show you a godly mind in a man aged and advanced in years?"

And I asked him to do this. Then that holy man called from the second table a certain man whose name was Laurence, who had spent forty-eight years in monastic life and was the priest next after the chief of the priests,
and he came up and bent his knees to the abbot, and the abbot blessed him, and when he rose, the abbot gave him no answer,
but left him standing before the table without eating, and this was just at the laying of the table, and he remained standing until the clearing of the table,
and I was ashamed to look at his face, for he was very old, about eighty-two years of age;
and when we rose from the table, the father sent him to the great Isidore mentioned earlier, to recite to him the beginning of the thirty-ninth psalm: "With patience I waited for the Lord."

But I did not neglect this; rather, I wished to draw out the old man, and I asked him what he had been thinking in his heart while he stood before that table. And he said to me: "I set it before myself in this way,
and I pictured the shepherd in my mind as Christ, out of my great faith in him. And it did not enter my mind at all that he was commanding me, but rather God.
And for this reason, father John, I stood not as before a table of men, but as before the altar of God, to pray to God,
and I did not conceive any evil thought at all against the shepherd, because of the abundance of my faith in him and my love for him, as it is written that love thinks no evil;
and know this, father John, that when a person gives himself over to simplicity of his own will, the enemy will find no place in him,
nor any time." As that good shepherd was, such a steward did the righteous Lord give him, a holy and meek man, such as is rarely found.
But one day that great father became angry at this man just mentioned, without cause, and ordered him driven out of the church; but I knew that he was innocent
of the matter for which the shepherd was rebuking him, and privately I spoke to the father about the steward, saying that he was innocent.

But that blessed man said to me: "I too know, father, that he is innocent; but just as it is not right to snatch bread from the mouth of a small hungry child, so too are wronged [?] by the soul of the shepherd

the souls of the strugglers who are under his hand, if he is not diligent to seek out for them occasion for crowns at every time, as much as they are able to bear: whether by abuse, or by reproach, or by contempt, or by humiliation. For he does harm by three great things:
first, because he deprives him of that reward which is given through the shepherd's rebuke; second, because it was possible from another virtue [?].
the benefit of others, and not doing it. Third, which is harsher than these: lest those who were thought to be patient and burden-bearing be made negligent by the shepherd,
if for some time, as though they were pleasing to him, he should neither rebuke them nor put them to shame, and in this way they should lose the meekness and patience that they had.

For though land may be good and fruitful and rich, yet often the lack of the water of insult and shame makes thorns spring up in it, and the bull's-head weed of arrogance, fornication, and fearlessness.
And the great apostle Paul knew this, and for this reason he writes to Timothy,

that [?] And I said to the elder that this generation of ours is weak, and that many stumble at rebuke that is not true, or even at that which is true, and separate themselves completely from the flock.
But that all-wise man
answered and said to me: A soul that has been bound to the love of its shepherd for the love of Christ, and has been filled with faith toward him, will not separate from him even unto death;

and all the more if it has also benefited from him through the healing of its wounds, but will always remember the saying that [?] But whoever has not been thus attached and bound and nailed to that love, I think that for such a one to remain in such a place is vain and useless, for he is joined to an erring and untrue obedience.

And that great man was not lying in this, but he was a powerful teacher, and one who accomplished and offered to Christ unblemished sacrifices. Let us hear the wisdom of God, and let us marvel at what is found in vessels of clay;

for when I was there, I marveled at the patience of many newly arrived men, which they showed under the humiliations and insults of the superior, and many times under persecutions as well, and not from the superior alone, but also from those younger than they.
And for this reason I questioned a brother for my benefit, who had been fifteen years in that monastery;
and his name was Cyrus, for I saw that the brothers constantly tormented him, and the servers many times drove him out from the table,
for that brother was by nature, in some very small degree, unable to restrain his tongue.
And I said to him: Why do I see you thus every day driven out from the table, brother Cyrus, and sometimes you even go to sleep without eating?
And he said to me: Believe me, father, these fathers are testing me, whether I am fit

to be a monk, and they do not do this to me in earnest, and I know their intention and that of the elder, and for this reason I endure everything without pain. And behold, for these fifteen years I have kept in mind what they told me at the very beginning, when they were bringing me into the monastery,
that they test those who become monks up to thirty years; and they do rightly, father John, for even gold does not become perfect without being tested.
And after my departure from that monastery, the valiant Cyrus remained two years and then went to the Lord, and at the time of the going forth of his soul he said to the fathers:
I give thanks to Christ, my fathers, and I am grateful to you as well, for since you were testing me for the sake of my salvation, I have remained untested by demons for these seventeen years.
And he died like a martyr, and that good shepherd buried him worthily with the saints buried there. I would be depriving those who are zealous for good things,
if I kept silent about the virtue of Macedonius, the archdeacon of that monastery. This man, worthy of praise,

once begged the shepherd, two days before the feast of the Epiphany, to send him to the city of Alexandria for some need of his own, and he promised to return before the feast in order to celebrate it.
But the devil, the hater of good, detained that archdeacon, and he did not return as he had promised the superior;

and one day after the feast he came to the monastery. And the superior removed him from his rank and placed him in the place of the newcomers. But the archdeacon accepted the father's command with patience. And with joy
and without distress, as if it were someone else and not he who was undergoing the punishment, he remained in that rank for forty days, and then the superior raised him again to his own rank;
and after one day he begged the superior
to return him again to that same former disgrace, and he said, "I committed a grievous sin in the city."
But the elder knew that he was seeking this out of humility, and that holy man gave leave to this good desire of his.

And I saw that old man, worthy of honor, standing with the youths and newcomers, and he begged each one to offer prayer for him, and he would say, "I have fallen into the fornication of disobedience."
And the great Macedonius himself told me why he desired this state of humility, and he said:
"Never have I seen in myself such relief from battles and such sweetness of that divine light
as I have seen in these days." It belongs to angels never to fall, and to human beings to fall and immediately rise again, however many times this may happen; but it belongs to demons,

after falling, never to rise at all. [?] of a certain monastery, he told me: "When I was young, I was employed in the care of the mules, and some spiritual fault and error befell me. But I had the habit of not hiding that serpent within me,
and I held it by its tail and revealed it to the physician. But he smiled and struck me lightly on the cheek,
and said to me, 'Go, child, to your service, just as you were, and do not be afraid at all.'

And I believed this with fervent faith, and after a few days I became fully assured that I was healed, and I went on in my service with joy and trembling." Every order and work of created beings has its distinctions,
and likewise in the community of those brothers there were differences of works and of minds. Therefore, when that physician perceived that some were making a show at the coming of lay people,

when such an occasion arrived, he would expose them before those who had come, and with shame he would reproach and humiliate them and assign them to a despised service. And thus he would strip them of this until, whenever they saw lay people, they would flee from them;
and a thing beyond nature could be seen, for vainglory was driving itself away,

and he hid himself from people. May Christ not deprive me of the prayer of that spiritual father, for one week before my departure from that holy place, the second in rank to that shepherd fell asleep in the Lord.
This man was wondrous, and his name was Menas. He had spent fifty-nine years in that monastery, and he had served in every kind of service.

On the third day we were performing the office for the departed one according to the rule, and during the morning prayer a fragrance was suddenly given off, and it filled the whole place in which the holy Menas was buried.
Then the father ordered that grave to be opened, and we saw that from both his feet, as from two springs, a blessing (eulogia) was flowing. Then the abbot said to the assembly: See

that the sweat of his feet and his labor have been offered before God as true myrrh. Those fathers also told me many other good deeds of the holy Menas, and they said this too: that once the abbot wished to test his patience,
which had been granted to him by God. When he went up to the abbot in the evening and bowed down, falling to the ground,
and asked for his prayer, as was his custom, the abbot neglected him and left him lying fallen on the ground until the ringing for matins,
and only then blessed him;
and he called him a show-off and impatient, and in this way raised him up. For that holy man knew that he would endure with courage, and for this reason he did this to him for the benefit of many.
And the disciple of the holy Menas told me

that he asked him whether sleep had come upon him as he lay below with bent knees before the abbot. And he told him: I completed the whole Psalter of David lying on the ground. I will not leave this crown of discourse unadorned by this emerald as well. For once I began to speak about stillness with some of those holy elders,
and they, with cheerful faces and kindly manner, answered me: We, Father John,

since we are weak and material, have taken up a life suited to our measure, and we have judged thus: that we should enter into battle according to the measure of our weakness. And we have considered the battle with people lighter,
who are sometimes angered and sometimes grow calm and comfort us, than that with demons, who are always armed with wrath against us. And one of those holy men, who
had great divine love toward me and boldness, said to me cheerfully and sweetly: O wise one, if you have firmly established within you the measure and the deed of him
who said that, if the Holy Spirit and the dew of holiness have come upon you, as he came upon the Virgin Mary.

And if you keep covered the power of patience from on high, gird your loins, as Christ God did, with the towel of obedience, and rise from the supper of your stillness, and wash the feet of the brothers with a humble mind. And set strong and watchful doorkeepers, unsleeping, at the doors of your mind, and hold fast that uncontainable mind within the body, in the unceasing service of the brothers.
Acquire stillness of mind with a body that moves about without rest in obedience; become quiet in soul amid the tumults of the people.
Put a bridle on the tongue that is quick to anger and dispute; fight that evil tyrant, the belly, seventy-seven times a day,

and nail to that wood of the soul, raised up in the form of a cross, the mind made firm like an anvil, so that it may be struck with sledgehammers and hammers whenever it is blamed and reproached, shamed and beaten,

and may not be loosened at all, nor be shattered, but may remain smooth, without lumps, and unshaken. Cast off your own will from yourself like a garment of disgrace, and, stripped of it, enter that place of struggle, for few are found to be thus.
Put on the chain mail of faith, so that it may not be loosened by unbelief nor be wounded. Hold the bridle of purity with both your hands against boldness,
which is improper touching. Bridle with the discipline of death the eyes, which wander about to gaze on the goodness and beauty of bodies;
rein in the mind that judges its neighbor, and turn it back to the care of itself,
and give it love, compassion and mercy as its work, and by this let all know, O beloved father, that truly [?] of brothers [?].
And stand thus in the community, and thus at all times [?] mockery as if it were living water, for David examined
every love that is under heaven and every beauty, and last of all said in wonder:

But if until now we have not been made worthy of the good things of such patience and obedience, then it is good that we should know our weakness and stand by ourselves far from the arena of those who struggle, and that we should call those strugglers blessed and pray for their patience.
But I was defeated by that father and good teacher, who contended with me from the Gospel and the prophets, with love.
And we gave preeminence and victory to honorable and glorious obedience without doubt. Let me recall one more virtue of those saints, and so let me depart from telling of their deeds,
as if from paradise, and begin to speak my own worthless and unprofitable words to you, who have gathered me by the sight of their virtues.
We were once standing at prayer, and that shepherd looked at certain brothers who were conversing in the church,
and he removed them from the church for seven days, and commanded them always to bow the knee to those coming in and going out. And this was the wonderful thing:
that both were priests. I saw one brother standing at prayer with a more fervent heart than all,
and especially at the beginning of prayer, as if he were conversing with certain people. I asked him about his thought, and for the sake of benefit he concealed nothing, but said to me:
"Father John, I have the custom of gathering my thoughts and mind together with my soul at the very beginning of the chanting, and I cry out to them, and call them, and say:"
I saw their cellarer, for small tablets were hanging from his belt. I inquired and learned that he wrote his thoughts on them, and he holds them out before that shepherd,
And not only did he do this thing, but many others who were there did so as well, for this was the elder's command. Once that shepherd expelled one of the brothers,
because he had spoken ill of a brother to him, saying that he was a chatterer and a great talker,
and that brother stood outside the monastery for seven days,
and begged him to forgive him and bring him back into the monastery.
And when it was made known to that soul-loving superior that he had eaten nothing at all during those seven days, he then sent to him and said: "If you wish to be in the monastery,

I will place you in the order of the penitents." And when he saw that he accepted this with joy, he ordered him to be taken to that separate monastery, where those were who mourned for their sins. And since I have mentioned that monastery, I wish to say a brief word about it too. There was a place about one mile distant from the great monastery, whose name was the Prison, and that place is without consolation:
no smoke is ever seen in it at all, nor wine, nor oil, nor anything else, except bread and uncooked herbs. And into that monastery he would confine
those who, after coming to be monks, fell into sin, each one by himself, or two by two, until God should give assurance concerning each one;
and he had set over them a great man named Isaac,
who urged those who were entrusted to him to pray continually, and he had palm branches,

which he would give them to work on, to drive away despondency. This is the work and the life and the conduct of those who truly [?]. He who marvels at the labors of the saints does well, and he who emulates their deeds saves himself; but he who wishes to carry out all their deeds at once goes astray, for he will not be able to.
