and they hear only dreams and the sounds of thieves, and are harmed by none of them, for humility is an untouchable treasure. Behold, for the sake of the blossoming and small growth of this ever-delightful fruit I have dared to speak a little wisdom;

but as for what the full stature and fruitfulness of that priestly-beautiful [?] one of the Lord is, ask those servants of the Lord, and he will tell you, for I do not have the power to show it in words. Concerning the riches and height of this blessed one, telling is impossible.
And a word about its nature is altogether inconceivable;
but about its forms we shall speak, according to the power of our understanding. Between true repentance and mourning cleansed
of every stain, and the all-holy humility of those newly come,
there is as much difference from one another as there is among flour, dough and bread; for the soul is crushed and ground by true repentance;
and it is joined, as it were, and, if I may put it this way, kneaded together toward God by the water of those good tears, and then the fire from the Lord is kindled within it,

and that blessed humility is baked and made firm, unleavened and not puffed up. Therefore this blessed threefold chain becomes one power and is united, and even more so the rainbow, and its works and powers are also united,

and whatever you say of one of these three as belonging to it will be found to belong also to the second and the third; therefore I will show this briefly before you. The working of this good and glorious trinity of virtues:

the first is this: the acceptance and bearing of every insult and contempt with joy; when, with the outstretched hand of the soul, a person accepts and embraces as sweet every reproach and shame, as medicines that make the diseases of the soul vanish,

and that blot out great sins; the second form of that good three-powered virtue is the complete killing of anger, contrition of heart, and blaming oneself in everything; and the third good ladder is, regarding one's own virtues,
complete disregard and disbelief, and a constant desire for instruction, with faith. And of the prophets; and [?]
The end of all unclean passions is vainglory and pride, whose slayer is
this holy and blessed stag, and it protects its companion, with whom it dwells, untouched by every deadly venom; for where in it could the venom of double-mindedness and evil-speaking appear?
Where could the evil serpent hide in its heart, and not at once be exposed and killed?
Nor in union with it is there any sight of hatred, nor any form of disobedience and disputing, unless the word is for the sake of orthodoxy,

against unbelievers. Whoever is united with this blessed one becomes Sweet, Kind, Merciful, and Calm, and Radiant, Untroubled, Vigilant, Diligent, and why should I say many things? He becomes unharmed by every passion, for it is said that [?] and from passions and battles. A humble monk does not search into hidden and unspeakable matters;
but the proud one investigates the judgments of God. Demons appeared face to face to a certain spiritual monk and called him blessed, but that all-wise elder said:
If you cease praising me, I shall know from your departure that I am great; but if you do not cease praising me, then I shall know from your praise my lack of holiness;

So now, if you depart from me, I would myself have become great; but if you praise me, I shall gain humility through you. And they were astonished at his victory on both sides and at his wisdom, and they vanished.
Brother, let your soul not be a cistern of this living water, which at times wells up and at times dries up from the heat of vainglory and haughtiness,
but let it be a spring of dispassion, always sending up the water of contrition. Know, beloved, that the humble soul is a valley among the mountains of labor and virtues,
remaining unshaken and unexalted. I did not fast,
nor did I keep vigil, nor did I lie upon the ground;
but repentance raises up and exalts the soul, and mourning knocks at the gate of heaven, and blessed humility opens it;

And I say and worship the threefoldness in one essence and the one essence in Trinity. The sun illumines everything visible, and humility strengthens every work of virtue. If there is no light, everything is dark, and if there is no humility, all our labor is vain. One [?] among [?]
which once saw the sun, and there is one thought, which many times begets humility. In one [?]
they rejoiced; and this is one virtue which the demons cannot claim for themselves. One thing is haughtiness, and another is not being haughty;
and another thing is humility, for the first judges others every day;
and the second judges no one, yet does not condemn himself either; but the third is uncondemned, and always condemns himself. Humility is one thing,
and striving toward humility is another; and the praise of the humble is another.
For the first belongs to the perfect; and the second to the truly obedient;
and the third to all believers. Whoever is humble within, such a one is not stolen away by his own lips, for what does not lie in the treasury

does not come out through the door. A horse, as long as it is alone, thinks that it is swift, but when it enters the racecourse, then it recognizes its weakness. When a man [?] natural things [?], this is a sign that he knows [?] healing;
but as long as he smells the stench, he cannot smell fragrance. All-holy humility said: Let my lover judge no one, nor dispute, nor love glory, nor accept leadership, until he is united to me,
for once he is joined to me, from then on for him [?]. A certain monk
who was eager to acquire this blessed thing, the demons came upon him and sowed praise from themselves in his heart; but the blessed one
employed a good means of overcoming them: he got up and wrote on the wall of his cell the names of great and lofty virtues,
such as perfect love, and angelic humility, and pure prayer, and inexpressible purity, and others like these.

When his thoughts began to praise him, he would say: Come, let us go to the reproof; and he would go and read those names, and say to himself: O wretched one, when you have acquired all of these, even then you are still far from God,

But since you do not yet have any of these things, how can you be proud? What the power and essence of this cause is, we are unable to say; but from its works and habits, and from the visible features of its image, let us say a little about its essence as well. Humility is a covering of God,

and the failure to see one's own virtues. Humility is an abyss of contrition, untouchable by all the thieves who steal the fruits of the soul. Humility is a strong tower, and all the more so when the thought of the heart has humbled them [?]. There are other signs in the soul of the one who possesses this blessed virtue,
apart from all those works mentioned earlier, by which he recognizes the wealth of his soul;
for all those that we mentioned earlier are visible to human eyes and are spoken of by people; but those signs

that come about in the soul of the humble person are inexpressible. Then you will know that this blessed virtue truly dwells in you, when your heart is filled with the abundance of that inexpressible light, and an indescribable love for prayer is in you, and, before these things, a heart that judges no one for sins and errors.
Its forerunner is hatred of all vain pride and of glory from people. Whoever has come to know his own weakness with true knowledge of the soul has sown his seed on good ground,

for if it is not sown in this way, humility will not blossom there. He who has recognized his weakness has attained the fear of the Lord, and going forward in it he will reach the gates of love. Humility [?]: those who draw near to it, it leads in there,

for I think it was on this account that the Lord said that whoever comes to this door from this world [?] without fear and [?] green pasture in the paradise of delight. All who come to monastic life by another way [?]. Let us examine ourselves well, we who are eager and desirous of finding humility; and if we find that our soul, with all its eagerness and strength, wishes that our neighbor

should be better and more honored than ourselves in everything, then let us know that mercy is near. As fire is not found in snow, so neither is humility found among heretics. This virtue belongs to the orthodox,
and to those who have been holy and God-loving. Many of us call ourselves sinners,
and perhaps we even regard ourselves so; but insult from others tests the humility of the heart. Whoever is making for this harbor free of waves, let him not cease examining deeds and words,
and thoughts, and ways of acting, and places and modes of life that are lowly and humble, until, with the help of God, through such deeds, he is saved from that ever-surging sea of pride,
and brings the boat of his soul out from there; for whoever is saved from this evil alone will quickly find forgiveness for other sins,

like that publican. For some, the sins they committed earlier, even after they have been forgiven, are a constant reason for humility, and by them they crush the evil neck of pride. Others remember the sufferings of Christ, and by this they humble themselves and regard themselves as debtors. And others crush their hearts by the errors that come upon them day by day;
And others, through the trials and illnesses that befell them, have drawn to themselves that mother of the virtues. But there are some, and I do not know whether they still exist now,
who, however much they advance through the gifts of God, humble themselves
and consider themselves unworthy of such wealth, and they are as though day by day their debt

were being multiplied. This is humility, this is blessedness, this is that perfect measure. When you see someone, or hear of someone, who has attained lofty dispassion in a short time, do not suppose that he arrived there by any other way than by this blessed, short and unerring road. O what good spouses are humility and love,
for the first exalts people, and the second no longer allows the one exalted to fall, for love never falls. Contrition is one thing,
knowledge of oneself is another, and humility is another. Contrition is the offspring of falls, for whoever falls is broken,
and he stands trembling at prayer with a praiseworthy shamelessness, leaning on the staff of hope like one who has grown weak, and with it he drives away the power of despair. Knowledge of oneself
is the unerring recognition of one's own measure,

and the constant remembering and searching out of one's sins, even in small detail. Humility is the invisible teaching of Christ, which dwells invisibly in the soul of the worthy and cannot be expressed in visible words. Whoever says that he catches even a slight scent of the fragrance of such an ointment,

and yet at the time of praise his heart is stirred even a little toward that praise, and he loves those words, let such a person not reproach [?] himself, but let him understand that he is entirely in error. I heard from a certain man, who said with the fervor of his soul, that [?]

For he knew that this nature of ours is unable by itself to keep itself free of passion. And again he said: That is, that in that age [?], for until I arrive there and hear the praise that comes from You, I have counted this praise of this world as nothing,
and rather as harmful. If this is the utmost limit of pride, that a person, for the sake of human glory, should lay claim to virtues that he does not have,
then surely it is a mark of great humility when we do not deny faults that we have not committed if someone accuses us of them, or when we even claim them of our own accord. So did

the one who took bread and cheese in his hand and sat at his gate astride a beam, and he displayed such humility; and likewise that other laborer of purity, who stripped off his garment and walked dispassionately through the city. Such people do not care about the offense taken by others,
for they have received through prayer the power invisibly to reassure everyone. Whoever is concerned about the first
betrays his lack of the second, for where God is ready to grant what is asked, there we are able to do everything. Let us choose this, brothers, that we may be pleasing to God

and not to people, for God rejoices greatly when he sees us seeking contempt from people, so that we may constrict and destroy that vain arrogance. True exile is the bringer [?] of such good things as these, for it comes about from one's own people,

[?] of insult and shame belongs to the very great. Do not be amazed at these things that have been said, beloved, for there is no one who has climbed to the top of a ladder in a single step. We are [?]
not when demons contend with us,
but our [?]. Natural fruitlessness raises upward the branches of the tree called citron, but when they are bent downward they immediately become fruitful.

Whoever reads with understanding has grasped this saying. The ladder of this blessed virtue too has received from God ascents of thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold, and the last of these the perfect climb,
the middle one the zealous, and the first all are able to climb. Whoever knows his own measure will never go astray by undertaking a task beyond his strength,
and such a person has set his foot on this blessed road. As a hen fears an eagle, so the humble person fears answering back. Without prophecy and signs and miracles, many have entered the kingdom;

but without humility no one will enter that bridal chamber. For those first things, this second one is the active guardian; but this second one has many times been made to vanish by those first things among those who are light-minded. This too the Lord arranged for our humbling: for no one sees his own wounds as

another person does. Therefore we ought not to teach ourselves, but to be taught by a spiritual shepherd, and when we are healed of our wounds, to give thanks to God and to him. The humble person always loathes his own will as a deceiver, and regards himself as ignorant;

therefore with humility he asks God for what is better, and with faith he learns what is good from him. The humble person is always obedient and listens to a better word from others, for he never trusts himself, but leaves his care to the Lord,
who opened even the mouth of the ass against Balaam. And even if he does and says everything in a godly way,
he still does not believe in his own understanding; for as asking others seems a burden to the proud, so does trusting himself seem to the humble. I think this:

that it belongs to angels alone not to be taken captive by sin, since even that great angel of the earth, Paul, said that [?]. For this reason we too must always hold judgment and blame against ourselves,
so that by voluntarily humbling ourselves we may escape those involuntary sins;
but if we do not do so, at the hour of death we will be grievously punished for them. Whoever asks a petition of God and holds himself unworthy of that petition,

he will receive more than it. A witness to this is that publican, who asked for forgiveness and found justification. The thief asked only to be remembered in the kingdom, and he inherited all of paradise.
Just as there is not seen on earth, nor is there found, a small and a great nature of fire,

for its whole nature is one, and even if it is a small coal, in nature it is equal to a great furnace; so true humility, wherever it settles, does not allow the matter of sin to exist there. As long as we sin willingly, it is not found in us;
therefore the Lord, knowing that outward form brings the soul to humility, took a towel and showed us the means and the way of humility,
For the soul conforms itself to its deeds,

and as its deeds are, so it is shaped. Authority became for one of the angels a cause of pride, though that authority had not been given to him for this. The mind of one sitting on thrones is one thing;
and that of one lying fallen on dunghills is another. Was it not for this reason that the great and righteous Job sat on the dunghill outside the city?
For it was then that he acquired perfect humility, and he said with knowledge of the soul:
I find Manasseh more sinful than all men,

who defiled the temple of God and all its worship with idols, and for whom, even if the whole world had fasted, it would not have been enough for his repentance; but humility was able to heal the incurable. David says to God: the rod of fasting [?]. Once the blessed one cried out
to humility, because of adultery and murder, and immediately he heard that [?]. The blessed fathers called bodily labors the way of humility;
but I say also obedience and sincerity of heart,
which by nature stand opposed to haughtiness. If pride turned some of the angels into demons, surely humility is also able to make angels out of demons;
therefore let the fallen not despair. Let us hasten, brothers, and strive with all our strength to climb up onto the head of this desirable one;

and if we cannot reach her head, let us at least sit on her shoulders; and if we are too lame to climb even there, then at least let us not fall from her arms, for whoever falls down from there, I do not know whether he will meet with any divine grace. Her roots and ways, but not her images, are poverty and living as a stranger;
the concealing of wisdom, and the begging of alms; the hiding of noble birth; the banishing of boldness, and separation from much talking,
for nothing humbles the soul so much as the form and life of beggary and contempt,
for our love of God shows itself when it is in our power to be exalted,

and we flee from bodily exaltation without turning back. Whenever you arm yourself against some passion, take this good humility with you as a helper, for then it is as though you have made sin and despair vanish,
and have trampled down the devil and these dragons, the flesh, by the power of Christ.
Humility is a ladder that raises the soul up to heaven from the abyss of sins. Someone saw her beauty in his heart, and amazement seized him,
and he asked her to tell him the name of her parent. And she, with a radiant and joyful face, said to him:
Why do you ask the name of my parent, since he is wondrous and nameless? I will not tell you his name

until you have acquired God dwelling within you, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. The mother of water and of the spring is the abyss, and the mother of understanding and discernment is humility.

Discourse of the same blessed John on diacrisis, that is, the understanding and discernment of thoughts, passions and virtues. Chapter 26. Discernment and understanding for those newly come to the monastic life is this:
that they truly understand their own measure and their own conduct; and for those in the middle it is this:
that they acquire a rational perception that unerringly distinguishes the truly good from what is natural and from what is opposed to it;
But among the perfect it is a light of understanding that has come from the divine radiance, which
is planted by God in the mind, and by its own light is able to illuminate the darkness of others as well;
or else, this is discernment for all, for beginners, those in the middle, and the perfect: the unerring finding of the will of God, so that at every time and place and in every matter one may know
in what the will of God lies. This is found among those who are pure in heart, body, and mouth. Whoever has conquered the three has conquered the five as well,
but whoever has neglected the three will not prevail over even one of the five.

Discernment is an undefiled and pure intention and the knowledge of conscience, which is the mind that understands good and evil, which God planted in man as a reprover of evil. Let no one fall through lack of understanding into unbelief

when he sees or hears of some deed beyond nature, for where a deed beyond nature is established, for where God who is beyond nature is established, there greater deeds beyond nature come to pass. From these three causes, above all, is born
all demonic warfare among us: either from negligence, or from pride,
or from their envy. The first is pitiable and the second is wretched, but the third is thrice blessed. As counselor and rule in all things, after God, let us use our conscience,
so that we may know from which direction the breath of the wind is coming in,
and set our sails toward it. In every divine work of ours, the demons prepare three pits for us.
For first they fight us in order to corrupt us from doing good, and when they are defeated in this, they then strive that the work not be done in a godly way.
And when those enemies are defeated in this as well, they then come upon us secretly and call us blessed because we have accomplished the work in a godly way.
The enemy of the first is zeal and the remembrance of death; of the second, obedience and being despised; and of the third, constant reproach of oneself. Our [?],
our [?] the fire of God, for from then on there is no longer among us the warfare of former habits,
for [?] of all evil heat, and of darkness, and of the stirring of habits, inner and outer, visible and invisible. The demons continually strive to do the opposite of this thing spoken of before.
For when they have mastered the soul and darkened that light of the mind, from then on there is no longer in us wretched ones any vigilance of mind,
nor discernment, nor understanding, nor shame, but only mercilessness, senselessness, lack of discernment,
and blindness. This saying will be well understood by those who have turned back from fornication,

or have awakened from boldness, or have come to understanding from disorderliness: how, after their awakening from that blindness of mind and after the departure of that darkness, they are ashamed even of themselves in their mind over the words and deeds that they spoke and did
while they were in that darkness. If night does not first fall during the day of the soul, those thieves will not come in to steal,

They slaughter and destroy. [?] of the soul is the destruction of that natural good. Theft is when a person does what is evil and harmful as if it were good. Theft is the unperceived plundering of the soul. [?] of the soul is the death of the rational mind, through falling into evil deeds. [?] of the soul is the complete cutting off of hope after lawlessness.
Let no one plead weakness as an excuse regarding the fulfilment of the commandments of the Gospel, for there are many, brothers,

who have done even more than the commandment, and let this one convince us: he who loved his neighbor more than himself did not stop [?] at this, but did more than the commandment. Let them be comforted, and let them take courage, and let them take courage, those passion-ridden ones
who have humility alone, for even if they fall into all pits and are caught in all snares,
and grow weak with every disease, yet after their healing they will become luminaries and physicians and lamps and guides to all, and will teach the forms of that disease,

and from their own experience they will save those who are about to fall. If any are overpowered by their former habits and are able to teach by word alone, let them teach, and perhaps they may somehow be put to shame by their own words and begin to do good in deed as well; but let them not become leaders, but let them teach by word if they are able.

And perhaps it may happen with them as I saw with some who had fallen into the mire and were buried up to the neck, and were teaching all who passed by the manner of their falling in there, and begging them not to go along that road,
and fall into the same pit. And because of the care they took for the life of others, the Almighty delivered them also from that clay.
But if those passion-ridden ones willingly give themselves over to desire, let them show their teaching of such things by silence, for it is written that whoever [?]
Truly we are crossing a harsh [?] and difficult sea, O monks, full of many gales and whirlwinds, and whirlpools and rocks and beasts and robbers,

and waterspouts and evil waves. By the whirlwind of the soul let us understand that sharp and sudden anger, and by the whirlpool, despair, which surrounds the mind and hastens to bring it down into the abyss of destruction.
And by the rock, insensibility, which embraces evil as if it were good; and by the beast let us understand this heavy and wild flesh; and by the robbers, those evil demons of vainglory,
who carry off the cargo and the labor of our virtues.
And by the wave we mean the raging and glutted belly, which by its own violence delivers us to the mouth of the beast. And the waterspout is that plunging pride,
which lifts us up to heaven and brings us down into the abyss. All who study writings,
know which are the lessons of those newly come to learning, and which are those of teachers.
Let us take good care lest we spend a long time in learning and still be learning the alphabet, for this is a shame, when a person grown old in learning is still learning the alphabet.
The alphabet of monasticism is this: obedience, fasting, vigil, wearing sackcloth [?], sitting on ashes, weeping, confession,

Silence, humility, courage, the frost of cold, labor, wretchedness, being insulted, contrition, not remembering wrongs, love of the brethren, kindness, simple and true faith, freedom from the cares of the world, blameless hatred of parents, flight from the affairs of the world, innocence and voluntary poverty. The teaching of those in the middle, who are making progress in the monastic life, is this: freedom from vainglory, freedom from anger, wealth of hope, stillness, discernment, firm remembrance of judgment and of death, mercy.
Love of strangers, measured instruction, passionless prayer, hatred of material needs. This is the boundary and law of perfected souls:
With the fear of God, also a heart free from distraction, perfect love, a spring of humility, the passing of the mind over to God,
the entry of Christ into the soul, the illumination of undistracted prayer, an abundance of God's radiance, the desire for death,

hatred of this life, flight from the flesh; intercessor for the world, one who compels God to mercy, joined with the angels, an abyss of understanding, a temple of mysteries, a beholder of things unspeakable, a savior of men, a god to demons, a lord over passions;
master of the flesh, ruler of the mind, a stranger to sin, a house of dispassion, made like the Master, by the help of the Master himself.

The mind needs no small vigilance when the body is weak, for when the demons see us lying prostrate on our beds and unable, because of that weakness, to fight them, they hasten to come upon us with fierce attacks. Those who are in the world, when they fall sick, are attacked by the demon of anger and often even of blasphemy;
but those who are outside the world, if they have the necessities at hand, are attacked by the demon of gluttony and fornication;

and if they are in harsh and comfortless places, the tyrant of despondency and ingratitude torments them. I set my mind to observe the demon of fornication, and I saw that he added to the pains and aches of the sick, and in the midst of those pains and aches he produced arousal of the flesh and discharge,

and the thing was astonishing, for in the midst of fierce pains and aches the flesh raged and domineered. And I saw other sick people lying on their beds who, by the power of God and by compunction, were comforted,
and they no longer suffered, but were as though no longer [under] the affliction of that disease, a deliverance [?];
and again I saw sick people

who through that sickness, as through some divine penance, were freed from spiritual sickness and evil passion, and I glorified Him who through the flesh made the flesh itself pure together with the soul. The rational mind has also been clothed with a rational perception,
which is within us and not within us; let us seek it unceasingly, for when it appears, these external stirrings will cease their work,
and this is why a certain wise man said: You have found divine perception.

Let the life of a monk be with understanding in every deed and word, in thought and in movement; for if it is not so, that life is not monastic, nor is it like that of the angels. Another is that of God,
And one thing is [?], and another is His [?], and another is His [?], and another is that which comes from [?]. And the first is over all created beings; and the second is for the faithful alone;
and the third is for the trustworthy and truly faithful; and the fourth is upon those who serve Him with zeal;
but the fifth is manifested upon those who love Him. Often a medicine that heals one person becomes deadly to another,

and often the very same medicine becomes beneficial to a person when he takes it at its proper time, and again, when taken not at its proper time, it becomes deadly to that same person. I saw a foolish physician
who afflicted a broken, sick man with reviling and with unseemly insults, and brought him nothing but despair; and I saw another, a skilled physician,
who with insult and reviling lanced a heart swollen with pride, and emptied out all its disease and stench. I saw the same sick man,
how at one time he drank the medicine of obedience, to purge the impurity of the passions, and went about and did not sleep,
and at another time the eyes of his soul grew weak, and he remained in stillness and did not converse. Some, I do not know how, for I have not

learned to inquire arrogantly into the gifts of God, but somehow, I do not know how, have by their very mind, so to speak, an inclination toward fasting, or love of stillness, or bodily purity, or lack of presumption, or gentleness, or compunction. And there are others
whose nature is opposed to these practices.
And they force themselves according to their strength,

and such people, even though they are at times defeated, yet, as those who do violence to nature, seem to me more pleasing than the former. Do not boast, O man, of wealth gained without labor, for the Giver of gifts knew beforehand your great [?] and weakness and defeat,

and by those free graces of His He gave you some small measure of salvation without your own labor. And even from childhood, upbringing and teachings and places either help us or oppose us with regard to virtue
and the monastic way of life. Angels are a light to monks, and true monks are a light to all people,

and for this reason we ought to strive in all things to be a pattern of doing good, in our word or in deed; for if the light becomes darkness, then how greatly will the darkness, that is, those of the world, be darkened! If you listen to me and obey me, it is better that we not scatter
our wretched selves in warfare of many kinds against the thousands, thousands upon thousands, and myriads upon myriads of our enemies, for we are not capable of searching out and finding their many

devices and machinations. Let us arm ourselves with the Holy Trinity against those three passions, and of the Holy Spirit [?], otherwise we shall bring many labors upon ourselves. Truly, if [?] comes also to ours [?], that our Israel too, which is the mind that sees God, may pass through that sea of the passions without drowning,
and may see those Egyptians, the passions, drowned in that water of tears,

but if he does not come to us [?], which is this flesh [?]. If God arises among us in deed, and if we hasten toward Him by beholding Him, then those of ours [?] will also become invisible. Let us hasten, brothers,
so that we may learn divine matters through labor and not by mere words, for it is not words that must be shown at the time of departure from this world,

but deeds. Those who hear of a hidden treasure hasten and take great labor upon themselves to find it, and when they find it they again take every labor upon themselves to guard it, for those who grow rich without labor will surely squander their wealth. It is difficult to do away entirely with the battle of former habits, and those who increase them and add to them have either cut off the hope of their own salvation, or have gained no benefit at all
from monastic life; although I know that all things are possible for God, and nothing is impossible for him. A question difficult to understand,
and beyond my comprehension, was put to me by certain people, one that I had found nowhere in the books I have read.
For they said: which of those eight thoughts are the offspring of the five among them? But I put forward praiseworthy ignorance in answer to their question;

and I begged them to teach me, and those blessed ones taught me thus: the mother of fornication is gluttony; and of despondency, haughtiness; while sadness is the offspring of all three, of gluttony, of love of money, and of vainglory; and anger likewise is the offspring of the same three. And the mother of pride is vainglory.
But I begged those blessed ones and said: Tell me this also: which are the offspring of those eight [?] thoughts? Or which one is the child of which?
And those dispassionate ones taught me gently, and said: There is no order or knowledge among the wicked, but only complete disorder and turmoil.
Those wise ones convinced me of this by extensive examples [?], a few of which we also write down here, so that from these few we may come to understand the others as well.
For they said: untimely and idle laughter is sometimes
born of fornication, and sometimes of vainglory, when someone inwardly takes wicked delight in himself; and sometimes of ease and comfort.
And excessive sleep is sometimes born of comfort; and sometimes of fasting, when the one who fasts grows haughty; and sometimes of despondency; and sometimes of nature.

And much talking sometimes arises from despondency and sometimes from vainglory; and despondency sometimes from comfort and sometimes from lack of the fear of God. And blasphemy is the offspring of pride, and many times it arises from judging a neighbor for that very thing; or it may also come from the envy of demons. Hardness of heart comes from satiety, and from pitilessness, and from idle love.
And idle love arises from fornication, or from love of money, or from gluttony;
or from vainglory, and from many other things. And perversity arises from loftiness and from anger; and duplicity from self-will and self-pleasing;
but the opposites of these are born of the parents opposite to those,

And so that I may not say much, for time would fail me if I wished to examine each one, let me say briefly that the true victory over all the passions mentioned earlier is humility; whoever acquires it has conquered everything. The parents of all evils are lust and wickedness, and these,

whoever has them shall not see the Lord; and we shall gain nothing from being rid of the first if we still have the second. Let us take rulers and wild beasts as our image of the fear of the Lord, and carnal passion as our image of the desire for him, for nothing prevents us
from taking a pattern for the virtues even from contrary things. This generation is filled with evil perversity, arrogance and hypocrisy,
for it displays bodily labors like those of the first fathers,
but it does not become worthy of their grace, although graces were never so needed by this nature as they are now. And this has justly happened to us, for not by labor,

but by simplicity and humility is God revealed in souls. Although the power of the Lord is revealed in weakness, the Lord will still not disregard a humble laborer. When we see one of the ascetic strugglers physically weakened, let us not seek out of malice to learn the judgment behind his weakness,
but rather, with good love, let us cherish him as our own limb, and let us receive him as a soldier wearied from battle and give him rest. Weakness often comes for the cleansing of sins;
and sometimes it comes for the humbling of the mind. When our good and sweet Lord and King sees someone slothful in ascetic struggle, he often humbles the flesh through weakness;
and sometimes, again, he cleanses the soul from passions and evil thoughts. Everything that comes upon us, whether visible
or invisible, can be received well, or indifferently,
or badly. I saw three brothers on whom some hardship fell: the first became angry, the second remained untroubled, and the third was filled with joy.
I saw a field sown by many laborers, and each one had a different thought. One had this thought, to pay off his debt; a second, to gain wealth;
another, to win the favor of his lord with a gift; another, to show his work to those passing along the road and receive praise from them;
another, to stir his enemy to envy and trouble him; another, not to be reproached by people for idleness. These are the kinds of seed those laborers sow:
fasting, vigil, almsgiving, service and things like these,
and let the brothers diligently examine those thoughts of which I speak. Just as when we draw up water we often bring up a frog along with it, so also when we practice the virtues,
passions too are often secretly interwoven with them. Let us understand it in this way: with hospitality is interwoven gluttony;
with love, fornication; with discernment, cunning; with wisdom, perversity; with meekness, laxity, sloth and self-will; and with silence, arrogance.
and to joy, haughtiness; to hope, negligence; to stillness, despondency and sloth; to virginity, irritability; to humility, boldness;

and with all of these, as a marvel, vainglory is joined. Let us not be distressed, beloved, when we ask something from the Lord and for a time He does not hear us. For the Lord would wish that all people might attain dispassion in a single moment.
But all who ask something from God and do not obtain what they ask, by one of

these causes this befalls them: either they asked before the time, or they ask unworthily and with vanity, or, if what they asked had been given to them, they would have become exalted or would have fallen into negligence. All know this, that demons and passions depart from us for a time,
or even entirely; but in how many ways they depart from us, I think few know.
The passions have departed from some, not only from believers but even from unbelievers, except for one; for they left that one with them,
as the leader of all evils and as filling the place of all the other passions,

whose wickedness is so great that it was able to make angels into demons. Again, the matter of the passions is consumed, burned up by the divine fire and made to vanish from the soul. Again, demons willingly depart from a person,

so that they may bring carelessness upon him, and then suddenly fall upon him and carry him off and plunge him into the passions, so that from then on he may become a fighter against himself. I know also another departure of demons,
when the soul has become accustomed to the passions. An image of what has been said is infants: once they have become accustomed to sucking the breast, then, even if they are weaned from the breast,
they suck their own fingers. I know also a fifth departure of demons and passions from the soul,
which comes about from simplicity and great and good innocence; for true and just is the help given by God to such people, and He delivers

them mysteriously from evils, like little infants who are often stripped while they are unaware of what is happening. Evil passion by nature has not been created in our nature, for God is not the creator of the passions; rather, the virtues were created by Him in us. For mercy is natural in us;
for this reason even pagans show mercy to people. And love is natural, for even dumb animals become sorrowful at separation from one another.
And faith is natural, for all of us have received faith from ourselves,
and we give birth to it in our souls. And hope is natural; for this reason too we receive baptism in hope;

and again, in bodily matters, in hope of enrichment we sow and [?], and go to sea. And since this is so, and love, which is a marvel and the end of the law and the prophets, is natural with us, then the virtues are in no way far from our nature; and let all be ashamed who say that it is impossible to practice the virtues. Above nature is the complete purity of virginity,
and freedom from anger, and humility and prayer, and vigilance, and fasting, and perpetual weeping and mourning.
Of these things, then, for some people the teachers and givers are men, for some angels, and for some the Word of God himself. When two evils present themselves, the lesser must be chosen,
as when we are standing in prayer and some brother comes, and we are obliged to do one of two things: either to abandon prayer, or not to see that brother and so distress him. Then indeed let us

understand that love is higher and more exalted than prayer, for prayer by itself is only one virtue, whereas love is what gathers together all the virtues. And again, I once came to a city in my youth. When I sat down at table, thoughts of gluttony and of vainglory beset me; but I was terrified of the offspring of gluttony, which is fornication,

and I let myself be overcome rather by vainglory. Among lay people the root of all evils is love of money, but among monks it is gluttony. Often God, by his providence, leaves certain small passions in spiritual people,

so that they may blame themselves over those worthless things of no account, and may gain the wealth that cannot be stolen, that of blessed humility. Newcomers cannot acquire humility without obedience;
for everyone who has learned a craft by himself is certainly conceited about it. In two virtues all the work of virtue is gathered together, as the fathers say, of which

the one releases from desires, and the other preserves that release from the passions forever through humility. For this reason mourning is twofold, for it undoes sin and brings in humility. This is the task of those who fear God: to give to everyone who asks of them,
but for people to give even to those who do not ask belongs to the more exalted;
and for people not to demand back from those who plunder them, and all the more, if they were able [?], this
is the work of the wholly perfect. Let us examine ourselves regarding all the passions and virtues, as to what measure we are at: the beginning, or the middle,
or the end. All the battles of the demons against us arise from these three causes: from love of pleasure, or from pride, or from their envy,

and those of the last kind are blessed, those of the middle kind utterly wretched, and those of the first kind entirely useless. There is a certain thought and awareness that is called the guarantor of hardships, and if it settles in a person,
he will no longer be afraid, nor will he turn back from struggle and bodily affliction. By this blessed thought the souls of the martyrs were seized,
and they easily despised their tortures. [?] Another thing is the guarding of the mind; likewise this second is higher than the first, even though it is harder. One thing is prayer about a thought,
another is answering thoughts, and another is counting them as nothing,
and to the first another testifies, the one who said [?] and the like of this,
and to the second testifies the one who
said that the adversary [?]; and again he says that [?]; but to the third practice the saying testifies that: [?]

; and again he says this: of these, the middle one often helps the first kind, when the thoughts find them unprepared and they are unable to answer; but the first is not able to do the work of the second kind, so as to drive away the enemies by means of it,
and as for the third, the demons disregard it entirely. By nature it is impossible for bodies to set a boundary for the bodiless, so that it could go nowhere outside that boundary,

but for one who has acquired God within himself, all things are possible through Him. Just as those whose sense of smell is healthy are able to detect if anyone is secretly carrying perfume with him, so too a pure soul is able to recognize in others both the fragrance that it has acquired from God,

and also the stench from which it has been set free, when it perceives them without the knowledge of those who have them. It is impossible for all to be free of passion, but it is possible for all to be saved and to be pleasing to God. Let those foreign offspring not have power over you,
who have wished, concerning the ineffable dispensations of God and his revelations, which he sends upon people,

to search them out, and who suggest inwardly that God is a respecter of persons. For they are wholly the offspring of pride. Sometimes the demon of love of money lays claim to humility; and again, sometimes the demon of vainglory urges us to give alms;
and likewise the demon of gluttony.
But if we become pure of these two in any way, let us not cease to give alms in every place. Some have said that there are demons opposed to demons;
but I have come to understand that all of them seek our destruction. The leader of every spiritual work, visible and invisible, is the thought and good desire, together with the help of God,
for if these do not go before, the virtues do not come into being. If there is [?], as the wise Solomon says,
and in all of it are also the works of this divine way of life of ours,

therefore let us understand this and seek each work in its own time, for certainly among those who struggle there is a time of freedom from passion, and a time of being subject to passion because of the immaturity of the strugglers. There is a time of tears, and a time of hardness of heart;

there is a time of obedience, and a time of leadership; there is a time of fasting, and a time of eating. There is a time of battle against those enemies of the flesh, and a time of the killing of that heat;
There is a time of spiritual winter, and a time of calm of mind; there is a time of sorrow of heart, and there is a time of spiritual joy; there is a time of teaching and a time of listening;
a time of defilement comes on account of pride, and a time of purity on account of humility.
There is a time of battle, and there is a time of rest;
there is a time of stillness, and a time of freedom from care, and of care, and of going out; there is a time of peaceful prayer, and there is a time of guileless service.
Let us seek nothing before its time out of pride; let us not seek in winter the work of summer;
nor, at the time of sowing, the work of reaping, for there is a time of sowing labors, and there is a time of reaping those ineffable graces.
But if we seek things before their time, we will not find them in their own time either. To some, after labor,
And some, at the time of death, received from God gifts and the rewards of their labors, by an ineffable dispensation.
It is therefore to be asked which of them, among these three, is lower than the others. There is a despair that comes from the multitude of sins and from the burden of conscience,
and from great sorrow, when the soul is sunk in its wounds and, from their weight, falls into the abyss of despair.

And there is again a despair that arises from pride and haughtiness, when a man thinks: "How could this error have come upon me? For I was not one deserving of such a thing." And whoever is attentive will find a distinct effect in these two: for the one gives himself over to disorderly living,
and the other to ascetic struggle with despair, which is incongruous.
But the first is healed by fasting and hope in God, and the second by humility and by judging no one. Let this serve you as a pattern and a rule in all ways of life
and in your deeds, whether you are under obedience or on your own, so that you may examine your every deed, visible or invisible, as to whether it is being done according to God.
-- And let us understand this as follows: we who have newly come, if we do some deed and humility is not added to us by it, more than what we had,
I do not think that deed was according to God, whether it be great or small. And this is the sign of God's will among us who are still infants;

and for those in the middle, the sign of God's will is the removal of faults; and for the perfect, the multiplying and increase of that divine light. Small errors are not small in the presence of the great;
but great ones, set beside the small, do not appear great. When the air is cleared of clouds, then the sun is seen purely;
and the soul, when it is made worthy of the forgiveness of its former sins, then sees that divine light well. Sin is one thing, negligence another, passion another, and a fall another;

let whoever is able search this out well with the Lord's help. Some bless wonder-working and prophecy above all spiritual gifts and graces, and do not know that there are many measures higher than these, which stand forever without falling.
Whoever has been completely purified sees the soul of his neighbor,

how it is, even though he cannot see the very essence of the soul; but whoever has not been made perfect, and is still making progress through bodily deeds, perceives also what belongs to the soul. A little fire often purifies all the material, and a small hole often empties out all the labor. Often, when this enemy, the flesh, is given rest, the strength of the mind stands firm, and the ruined fervor does not rise up again;
and again, often we have worn the flesh out with ascetic struggle, and evil stirrings are stirred up in us, so that we may not trust in ourselves,

but in him who invisibly puts to death these living enemies, the flesh. When we see certain people who love us for God's sake, let us be the more careful toward them, lest we become overly bold; for nothing so dissolves love and produces hatred as overboldness. It is beautiful and holy,

and the well-seeing eye of the soul; and after the goodness of the angels, it is higher than all nature. For this reason also the thoughts of those subject to passions, which are born in the hearts of others,

they are able to know through their love toward them, and especially when they are not defiled and submerged by these filthy bodies. If to him, like that material one [?], let whoever reads understand.
Those who also understand bodily trials as God's looking upon them;
but the perfect understand them through the coming of the Holy Spirit and the multiplication of graces. There are perfect ones who are strengthened by divine longing,

and with humility of heart they perform great virtues; and others undertake this work with pride and are put to shame. There is a demon who comes to us when we lie down on our beds, and hastens to wound us with evil and defiled thoughts;
and if we are negligent, and do not arm ourselves with prayer against him, and fall asleep amid those evil thoughts, we fall into foul dreams. There is also another demon,
who is called the forerunner and scout, who, when we wake up,

comes upon us and hastens to defile our first thoughts. Give the beginning of the day to the Lord, so that when it dawns, thoughts from him may settle in you, and not those from the devil, for whichever of them gets there first, to him that day will also belong. A praiseworthy saying was told to me by a good laborer of virtue:

that as soon as it dawns, I know how I am going to be that whole day. Many are the paths both of the service of God and of perdition; for this reason it often happens that what is contrary to one person comes well to another, and the deeds of both are pleasing before the Lord.
When some trial befalls us, then the demons fight against us, so that we might say something or do evil,
and when they cannot make us do this, then they approach us secretly and sow in us a thanksgiving full of pride. Some by that one part go up;
but those who think on earthly things go down, for of those who have been separated, no one remains in the middle. One has received existence together with another, and not alone,
and it is a wonder how, apart from that in which it received its existence,

it is able to be free of passion. Good daughters are borne by mothers, and the mothers by the Lord; and the opposing evil daughters are borne by their mothers, and their mothers by the devil. Fear, and still more God [?]; let not the last error
of the soul become worse than that first fall. The light of all bodies is the perceiving eyes;
but the intellectual light of the divine virtues is discernment and understanding.
Chapter two, on discernment and understanding itself. As the thirsty deer longs for springs of water, so the soul of monks longs to know the will of God, that good and excellent and perfect will,
and also the will mixed with it, and the opposing and evil will, about which our discourse is long
and hard to interpret; and also which deeds are needful,
so that they may be done swiftly and without delay,
according to that saying which says:
woe to him who delays from time to time.

Or which are the deeds that ought to be done calmly and with much deliberation? As that speaker teaches us, who says that [?], and again says that [?]. For not all are able easily to understand these things that are hard to understand, since even that God-clothed one,
who had the Holy Spirit within him,
prayed many times
about such matters as these; and at one time he said: [?], and again at another time
he said that [?], and again that [?] from all the cares and passions of this world, and I lifted up [?]. Those who wish to know the will of God
must put themselves to death, and they must pray with a simple and innocent heart, in faith;
and let them ask spiritual fathers or brothers, and let them accept what these counsel as from the mouth of God, even if that word is contrary to the thought of their own heart,

and even if those whom they ask are not very spiritual and discerning. For the Lord does not disregard souls who in faith and innocence have entrusted themselves to the counsel of the fathers, even if those

whom they ask are ignorant; rather, the one who speaks through them is the Lord, the All-wise and Good. Those who carry out the aforesaid practice, with joy and without doubting, are filled with much humility. For if someone used to open up parables with an instrument of song, how much higher is the rational mind

and the intelligent soul than that soulless instrument of song! Those who did not wish to carry out this aforesaid practice, but strove by themselves to know the will of the Lord, made use of many kinds and many forms of means.

These were told to us, and some of them I shall now relate. Some, when they had two plans of some kind and wished to know which was the will of God, removed their mind completely from all carnal love. And they restrained their mind, so that it would not
incline toward either one of the two;

and with fervent prayer, on appointed days, they presented to God their mind stripped of its own will, and in this way they found knowledge of his will: either an invisible mind spoke invisibly to their mind and told them the better course,
or one of the thoughts vanished completely from their soul. And others, again, from the trial of disruption that came upon the undertaking, understood that the disruption was from God,

in accordance with that speaker who said that [?]. And others, again, adopted a sign opposite to this: from the hardships and trials that came upon them in that undertaking they understood that the will of God was in it.

And others, again, understood from prosperity and success that God wills the thing, as it is said that God grants success to everyone who does good. As for one who has God within himself as his enlightener, his mind is itself enlightened by God, and he becomes confident about matters, whether each one ought to be done quickly or late.

For when a person is half-hearted about his deeds and cannot become whole-hearted, it is evident that his soul is still unenlightened and loves glory. There is no injustice with God, that he should shut the door on those who knock with humility and entreat him. In everything that we do, let us examine our thought, to see toward what it is inclined;
for every deed that we do for God, pure of every fleshly deed and thought,

will have a good end, even if it does not appear good; but if there is a fleshly thought in it, I do not know whether it will turn out for the better, for it is a thing to be feared. The judgments of the Lord are unsearchable, for many times, by his providence, he hides his will from us, because he knows that even if we were to learn it, we would have no intention of doing it. For this reason he does not reveal it to us at all, so that a greater punishment may not come upon us for not doing it. A sincere heart has escaped from the crookedness of affairs,

and sails without sinking in that boat of innocence. There are courageous souls who, out of divine love and humility of heart, undertake struggles beyond their strength; and again there are proud hearts who do the same.
For many times the demons make us eager to undertake deeds beyond our strength, so that because of this we may become fainthearted and fall away even from what we had the strength to do,
and become a laughingstock to our enemies. I have also seen weak souls and bodies,
who, because of the multitude of their sins, undertook struggles beyond their strength and could not bear them; I taught them and told them:

that repentance is accepted by God, the Creator of all, according to the abundance of humility and not according to the abundance of labors. Sometimes the place of one's upbringing becomes a teacher of many evils, and sometimes living among evil people, but more often it is wickedness of soul

and perversity of mind that becomes the bringer of perdition. Whoever is separated from these two is separated from the third as well, but whoever has the third is unproven in every place. For there is no place that has kept a person from sin if he does not take care himself. If unbelievers dispute with us,
or those who believe wrongly, out of an evil will, let us withdraw from them after one or two admonitions;

but if someone wishes with a sincere spirit to know the truth, let us not cease speaking what is good right to the end; yet let us do both according to the firmness and the measure of our souls. It is great folly if someone hears

of those deeds of the saints that are beyond nature and despairs of his own life; for he may gain two benefits, if he wishes: either he may take up zeal and courage to emulate what is good, or he may know himself and rightly understand his own weakness, through that blessed humility which is the bringer of good things. There are defiled demons,
more evil than the other demons, who not only fight against us to bring us to sin,
but also strive that we should make others share in that evil, so that we may be given over to a harsher torment. I saw a man
who learned an evil habit from another;

And that teacher came to an understanding of his deed, and he ceased from evil and came to repentance, but because of the sin of that disciple his repentance became feeble and difficult. Very great, truly, very great indeed is the wickedness
of those evil spirits, and it is known to few, and I think that not all of it is known even to the few. For how is it that at times, in ease and satiety, we are thoroughly wakeful;
but when we fast and struggle, we are pitiably sunk in sleep; when we are in solitude, our hearts grow hard;
and when we mingle with people, we become compunctious; when we are hungry we see evil dreams, and when we are full we see nothing. In the time of ascetic labor we are darkened;
and when we drink wine, we become compunctious and cheerful. Concerning all this,
let him who is able enlighten, by the Lord, the unenlightened, for we are unenlightened as to understanding such matters; but this we say: that such a change does not come altogether from the devil,
but sometimes it comes from the constitution of this nature which has been given to me, of this wretched flesh,

coarse and contrary. When any of these aforementioned things happens to us, then let us entreat the Lord with fervor and humility, and if after that entreaty we find things the same for a long time, let us know that it is not from the workers [of evil],
but the matter comes from nature,
or else it is some dispensation of God, and through contrary things he wills our benefit, so that in every way our pride
he might humble. Hidden and difficult is the searching out of that abyss of God's judgments, for those who search into such things are sailing in the ship of pride. A certain brother asked an elder,
one of those who see hidden things, and said to him: "Why did God, though He knew beforehand that some would fall, adorn
[?] they with gifts and miracles?
And he answered: First, so that he may make other souls cautious; second, so that he may show the free will of human beings;

and third, so that at the judgment to come he may leave those who have fallen without excuse. The old law, as being weak, said: [?]; but the Lord, as being strong, commanded us even to turn back a brother, and said: [?] and what follows. If your joy is pure and your teaching humble, carry out the word of the Lord, and especially with those who take it upon themselves.

But if you are not of that measure, then carry out that word of the law, and guard yourself. Do not be surprised if even those you love become hostile to you, for some are vessels of the devil, especially against his enemies. I marvel, beloved,
at one thing among our doings: how for the virtues we have help from God, who is able to do all things,
and from his angels and his saints;

while for evils only the demons are helpers, and yet we are more eager toward evils and passions. And for this reason I cannot say much, nor do I wish to. All created things, if they remain as they were created, are in that same nature,
just as I am the image of God and am mingled with this clay,
as the great Gregory the Theologian says; but if any created thing is outside that nature in which it was created,
without doubt it longs insatiably for that which is properly its own.
Let a man use every means and strive with all diligence to raise up this clay and seat it on the throne of God,
and let no one make excuses concerning that ascent,
for the way and the door stand open. Hearing of the spiritual virtues of the fathers awakens a man's mind and soul to imitate their zeal; and hearing their teaching

further stirs him to imitate them and to desire them, and leads those who have divine zeal to become like them. Discernment is a lamp in the darkness, a guide of those who have gone astray, and an enlightener of the blind. The discerning man is a finder of health,

and a destroyer and remover of pains. Those who marvel at the small deeds of others do so for one of two reasons: either from great lack of understanding, or from great humility, they magnify and exalt the deeds of their neighbor. Let us strive not only to fight,
but also to defeat the demons, for whoever fights sometimes wins and sometimes is defeated;

but let him who has wholly conquered go on conquering always. He who has become victor over the passions wounds and crushes the demons, and appears to them in outward form and likeness as though he had passion; and thus he deceives the enemies and remains unassailed by them
and without temptation. A certain brother was once treated with contempt and abuse by another, and he was not at all stirred to agitation in his heart, but prayed in his mind,
and then he began to cry out in a loud voice feigning passion, and made it appear that he was pained by that abuse, and

in this way he concealed his freedom from passion. Another brother, again, utterly hated sitting in the highest seat, yet he put on a show and made it appear that he was pained over this and wanted the high seat. How shall I tell you and explain the purity of him who went into the brothel,
and made it appear that he was going in for evil, but he drew even that harlot to chastity. To another solitary, someone brought at dawn an early-ripe bunch of grapes,
and when the one who had brought it to him had gone away, that elder at once fell upon the grapes and ate them without desire,

so as to show himself to the demons as a glutton. Another man, adorned with virtue, came to be short of a few palm leaves, and every day he made himself appear as though he were pained over those palm leaves, while he had no care for them at all. Such men as these have need of great wakefulness and caution. Let it not be, then, that while they wish to mock the demons, they themselves are mocked by the devil,
for these are the ones
of whom the blessed apostle Paul said, as [?] and they in righteousness [?]. He who wishes to present body and heart pure before Christ, let him keep freedom from anger and fasting;

without these all our labor is in vain. Just as the light of the eyes varies, and some see keenly and others deficiently, so too the comings of the perceptible [?] sun into the soul of man have many kinds of distinction. One is the joy that comes through bodily tears
into the soul [?], and another is that through spiritual tears; and one is that through bodily eyes, and another is that through spiritual eyes; one comes from hearing words;
and another is produced in the soul of itself; one comes from obedience, and another from stillness, and from all these distinctly;

It is another who, by the rapture of the mind, presents the soul before the light of Christ, in a way that cannot be told or expressed. There are virtues, and there are parents of virtues; so whoever is wise

is the more eager to acquire those parents. Of those parents the Lord alone is the teacher, by his own power, but of their offspring there are many others as well. Let us take care, then, that we do not,
when we fast, make up for the lack of food with sleep;

for this is what fools do, just as it is also folly to eat a great deal at the time of vigil. I have seen laborers of virtue who, on account of some hardship [?], gave way a little with regard to food, and immediately, standing all night long, those brave and valiant ones punished their belly and taught it to flee from satiety with joy. The demon of the love of money fights fiercely against those who have nothing, and when it cannot overcome them, it then brings up the poor as a pretext, and in this way compels those without possessions to become owners of possessions. When the spirit of despair fights against us,
then let us remember the commandment that the Lord gave to Peter, how he commanded him to forgive.
For he who commanded this of another, would He not
himself do even more? But when we grow haughty, then let us remember the saying that a spiritual being, over one passion, [?]
that is, haughtiness [?]. There are wicked spirits and envious demons who deliberately withdraw from the saints, so that they will not be defeated by them
and bring them a crown of victory. And no one disputes this; but I have seen someone who created enmity between two people, and I called him blessed.

There were two people who had a love of fornication for each other, but a certain wise and experienced elder created hatred between them; for he told each one tales about the other, saying to the first, "He is always slandering you and says evil things about you," and likewise to the second. And that wise man was able to undo the wickedness of the demons by a human stratagem, and he created a hatred that undid the fornication. There are people who, for the sake of one commandment, break another commandment;

for I have seen young men who loved one another in a godly way with a pure heart, and because of others' passion and conscience they made each other resentful and parted from one another for some time, so that no one would encounter a stumbling block. Just as the wedding day and the day
of being carried to the grave are opposed to each other, so here haughtiness and despair testify against each other; and often, through the disorder of the demons,
these incompatible passions are found together at one time in the soul, which is a marvel. There are certain unholy demons who teach us the interpretation of the Scriptures,
and they do this especially in the hearts of the vainly haughty, and above all of those who are educated in the learning of the philosophers;

and at first they begin by suggesting what is true, so that little by little they may lead them astray and cast them into heresy and blasphemies. When, at the time of such understanding, we see agitation, restlessness, and disorderly joy, from this let us know that this theology of the demons is fighting against God and not theology. Each created thing has received from the Creator its order and beginning,
and of some things there is also an end; but the limit and end of virtue cannot be reached, for the Psalmist says that,
and endless [?]. If I were to go in strength, that is, from the strength of action to the strength of contemplation,
and love never comes to an end anywhere,
and of fear, of love, whose end is endless; and if we advance in it, we shall never rest, neither in this passing world nor in that age to come
upon light, to receive yet other light and good understanding. Even though this saying may seem strange to some, yet I say, O blessed one,

that just as I said above that virtue is endless, so now too I say that not even those bodiless natures of the angels are without advancement and forever at one level, but they always ascend from glory to glory,
and upon understanding they ever multiply understanding. Do not be surprised if the demons even suggest something good to us and then themselves oppose our thoughts,
for they do this in order to persuade us that they know the counsels of our heart,

but far from it! Apart from what they themselves have suggested to us, they know nothing else. Do not be a harsh judge and an evil critic when you see some who are lofty and great in word, teachers and enlighteners of souls, but in deed not vigorous strivers,

for often the benefit of the word makes up for the deficiency of action. Not all of us have everything equally, for in some, word prevails over deed, and in others, deed prevails over words. God has not created evil at all,
nor has he made it at all,
and therefore some have erred who said that certain passions are natural in the soul, and they did not understand

that those things created good in our nature and for the benefit of nature, we have changed into passions; for by nature there is seed in us for the sake of children, but we have changed it into fornication.
By nature heart-
wrath, that is, anger, is in us against the demons, but we use it against our neighbor.
And again there is zeal in us by nature, so that we may be zealous for doing good, but we hold it for evil.

By nature there is desire in us, but for the Kingdom, and we have changed it for the sake of sin. And we also have loftiness by nature, but over the demons; yet we have taken it up where it is not proper.

And he has also given us joy by nature, but for the Lord and over the good of our neighbor, yet we have turned it upon evil. We also have remembrance of wrongs by nature, but against the enemies of the soul, and we have changed it against our brothers. The soul of the diligent rouses the demons to wrath against it,
but when battles multiply, crowns also multiply. [?] who will not become crowned either;
but he who does not despair over the falls that have befallen him, nor lets the battle rest, will be glorified by the angels as a brave soldier. He who
[?] in, he lives forever; but he who becomes victor over the three times will no longer be defeated, nor will he die forever. If, by dispensation, for the sake of our instruction,

After that intelligible [sun?] has risen among us again [?] from us, then there come among us those that had earlier departed from us: those wild creatures and all the beasts of that thicket, of the thorny passions of our hope [?], and they demand passions, or deeds, or thoughts. At the coming of humility among us, again [?] those spirits that love pleasures of taste,
and are no longer with us, those demons, so that we too may say again: "But you have fled pitifully." That is, the soul exalted above every earthly desire,
that is, the heart previously darkened by the passions; the idols are the evil thoughts of this mind. If our Lord Jesus Christ fled from Herod in the flesh, he who was able to do all things,

let the proud be taught not to hand themselves over willingly to temptations, for it says that loftiness is entwined with courage, as the plant called smilax is entwined with the cypress. With good examination let us examine ourselves, whether there is any true good in us,
and in this way we have found ourselves lacking in every true good. Search out unceasingly the form of the passions as well, and you will find that there are many within us,

which we cannot see, since we are weak in mind; but if the eyes of the soul are enlightened, then we will see them plainly, for as long as they rule over us we are not able to see them. God judges the intention,
but he requires deeds according to one's ability,

and all of this with love for humankind. Great is the person who does not fall short in doing the deeds that are within his ability, but greater than he is the one who in humility undertakes even those beyond his ability. Often the demons turn us away from very small deeds,

even those from which our profit would come, and urge us to do heavy deeds beyond our ability. You find concerning Joseph that he was made blessed for turning away from sin and not for being free of passion. It must be investigated for which and for how many sins the turning away has a crown; for it is one thing

to flee from darkness, and it is a greater thing to flee toward the sun. Darkness brings on stumbling, and stumbling brings a fall, and a fall brings death. Those darkened and fallen from wine have often washed themselves with water,
but those fallen from the passions have washed themselves with tears. Disturbance of the mind is one thing, agitation is another, and darkening is another;
and fasting heals the first of these, stillness the second, and obedience and the Lord Jesus Christ the third,

who [?]. Nothing prevents us from taking, as an image of the purification of the soul, those who cleanse material garments, for the fuller and the dyer cleanse and adorn these, and the spiritual fullery is the community of the monastery,

which cleanses the filth and coarseness and sins of the soul; and when within it the soul has stripped off all the coarseness of anger and the remembrance of wrongs, then stillness becomes for it a beautiful and richly colored dye. Some say that falling into the same former sins comes from a deficiency of repentance for those first falls; but it must be asked whether everyone who has not fallen into his former sins has repented worthily and fully. Some have fallen into their former sins,
because they plunged the former ones into the abyss of forgetfulness and did not remember the torments that are coming upon them on account of them;
or because, out of love of pleasure, they reckoned God to be a lover of mankind beyond measure; or else because they cut off the hope of their own salvation. But let no one reproach me if I do not
also say this: or because they could not bind this enemy, the flesh, which tyrannized over them by the force of habit. It must be asked how,
since the soul is bodiless and immaterial, it does not see the bodiless beings who come to it as they are; but perhaps this is because of that union

which only he knows who united them. A certain spiritual and learned brother asked me about a certain matter that I wish to learn, and said to me: "Tell me, which sins humble the mind, and which exalt it?"

And I confessed: "I do not know." Then he said to me: "I will place with you a little leaven of teaching, and afterward examine it well yourself: for fornication and gluttony and wrath and despondency and sleep cannot raise the horn of the mind; but love of silver and love of authority and much talking and judging others and many other things add evil upon evil and exalt the mind." Whoever has gone among lay people, or has received them in his cell, and after they have parted is struck by an arrow of sorrow, and has not rather become glad that he has escaped the snare and stumbling, such a one is being mocked by the demon either of vainglory or of fornication. First it befits us to see from which direction the winds are rising, so that when we raise the sail they may not become a hindrance to our journey. Comfort with love the laboring old men,
who have crushed themselves by the labor of fasting, and [?] a little rest. Compel to fasting the young, who have crushed
their souls with sin, and remind them of those everlasting torments. It is impossible, as we have said above, that having gone out from the world
we should be at once wholly cleansed of gluttony and pride;

but let us not fight pride with gluttony; rather, let us with fasting implore the Lord to deliver us from it, for the time is coming, and for those who so desire it is already here, when the Lord will subject this too beneath our feet. The young and the old who come to become monks do not have the same battles,

for their sicknesses are not the same; therefore blessed is longed-for humility, for it becomes an unerring repentance for both the young and the old. Do not be astonished at this word that I intend to say, for they are few, yet there are souls that are simple and innocent and ignorant of cunning and perversity,
Those for whom being with people is wholly opposed [to their good], for they are able, by living in stillness with their teacher alone,
as by a ladder to ascend to heaven, and to remain untouched and unharmed by the disturbances and tumults of monasteries. Those who love fornication,
people heal; and the wicked, angels heal;

but the proud, the Lord alone. This too is a form of love, and it often happens: when a neighbor comes to us, let us leave him to his own will in whatever he wishes, and in everything let us show him a cheerful face. Let us investigate
when repentance becomes a loosener of good things, as it is a loosener of evil things. Let us investigate and understand well when, or over what,

or for how long it is fitting for us to stand firm in the battle against the matter of the passions, for flight too may be chosen because of our weakness, so that we may not die. Let us see and understand
which demons exalt the mind, and which abase it;
and which harden, and which falsely lay claim to light; and which make us slack,

and which make us eager, and which invite us to sorrow, and which to joy. Do not be surprised if, when we come to be monks, at the beginning we see ourselves as more free of the passions [?] than when we were in the world;
for it is necessary that first those materials of the passions be stirred up and go out, and in this way health comes; or else those beasts were previously hidden within us, and we did not see them,

but now we have seen them. When something happens and those who have drawn near to perfection are defeated by the demons in some small matter, they strive by every means and make up for the matter a hundredfold. Just as winds sometimes stir the surface of the sea, when they are not violent, and sometimes again
churn it up from the abyss, so also are the passions: for in those subject to passion they cause disturbance from the depths of the heart;
