but in the perfect, only on the surface of the mind. And therefore they quickly regain that unforgetfulness of theirs. This is the task of the perfect: always to discern in their own soul which thought has come from conscience, and which is from God,
or which is from the demons; for the demons do not suggest everything as evil from the first, and for this reason it is difficult to discern this.
By two sensible eyes the body is illumined;
but the discernment of thoughts and of visible actions illumines the eyes of the heart.

Other chapters on the virtues. Firm faith is the mother of ascetic struggle, and its opposite is evident. Good hope makes one hate the world, and its opposite is evident. Love of God is the cause of living as a stranger,
and its opposite is evident. Obedience is born of self-accusation and of desire,
and of contempt. Fasting is the mother of health, and a reminder of death. The remembrance of death and training in the sufferings of Christ are helpers of purity. Stillness makes invisible
the heat of the flesh. Vigilance and fasting are crushers of evil thoughts,
of foul ones, and quellers of battles. Faith and living as a stranger are killers of the love of money;
and mercy and love know the giving even of their own body. Unceasing prayer is the destroyer of despondency;
and the remembrance of judgment,

[?] is the deceiver [?] of zeal. The remedy for anger is love of insult and disgrace; and psalmody, mercy and poverty are the quenchers of sorrow. Hatred of visible things makes one love the invisible;
and silence and solitary stillness are fighters against vainglory;

but if you are living in the midst of others, love contempt. Visible pride may be healed by a broken and lowly [?] way of life; but invisible pride by the Invisible One, he who was born before the ages. The deer is the killer of all visible reptiles;
and humility is the killer of all invisible beasts. There is one among natural things
that teaches us all invisible matters. As with that old skin, unless it enters a narrow hole [?]; so neither can we strip off our former habits and the defilements of the soul,
and the garment of the old man, unless we pass along that narrow and hard way of fasting and contempt. As a greatly fattened quail cannot rise to the height of the sky;
so too the one who fattens his flesh.
As swine cannot rest on dried-up mire;
so a contentious disciple perishes. As good iron sharpens soft iron, so a zealous brother often saves a negligent one. As an egg that is hidden in dung
also brings forth chicks, so the thoughts of the heart that you do not reveal, you will carry out in deed. As a horse in the arena, those that race against one another,
so is a gathering of good brothers. As a cloud covers the brightness of the sun,
so evil thoughts darken the mind. As one upon whom the sentence of death has gone out no longer asks about, nor says anything concerning, jesting [?] and singing,

so neither should a true mourner fill his belly. As the poor, when they see the treasures of kings, recognize their own poverty all the more; so the soul that reads of the lofty virtues of the fathers and martyrs has its mind humbled all the more. As iron obeys the magnet even unwillingly, so those who have become habituated to a passion

are overpowered by it by force. As oil calms the sea, so fasting quells the burning of the flesh. As water, when it is confined, rises upward, so a soul confined by battles and temptations rises by repentance toward God and is delivered from its oppressors. As one who has fragrant ointment,
even if he does not wish it, becomes known by its fragrance, so the one with whom the Spirit of the Lord is becomes known to all by his word and by his humility. As winds trouble the sea, so
anger, more than all diseases, troubles the mind. As a thing that the eye has not seen is not greatly longed for,
so those who are virgins in the flesh are lighter in their battles than those who have experience of evil. As the treasures of a king,

Thieves do not much dare to approach a place that has guards around it; so too, he who establishes prayer in his heart will not be much plundered by those invisible robbers. As fire does not come out of snow,
so he who seeks the honor of this world cannot attain the honor of heaven. As one ember often burns up a great deal of material,
so there is found one good deed that blots out multitudes of sins. As it is impossible to kill wild beasts without weapons,
so neither can anger be killed without humility. As human nature cannot exist without food,

so it is not fitting for a person to be negligent even for one moment until death. As the light of the sun, when it enters a house through a hole, illuminates everything, so that even the tiny dust is seen,
so when the fear of God enters the human heart, the person sees all his sins, open and hidden. As the crab sometimes goes forward and sometimes backward and cannot make straight progress,
so a soul that sometimes laughs, sometimes weeps, and sometimes indulges in pleasure will gain nothing. As it is easy to steal something from a sleeping person,
so those who are close to the world are easily stripped of good works. As one who fights a lion,
if he is negligent even for one moment, is killed, so he who fights his own flesh, if he gives it rest, will be defeated by it. As harm befalls one who climbs a broken ladder,

so all human honor and glory are opposed to humility. As it is impossible for a hungry person not to remember bread, so without remembrance of death and judgment, life is impossible. As water blots out writing,
so tears blot out sins. As some writings are not blotted out by water, and we blot them out by some other means,
so souls that have no tears are wiped clean by sighing, mourning, and great anguish. As dung multiplies worms,
so an abundance of food multiplies falls and evil and defiled thoughts. As one whose feet are bound,
cannot walk, so he who gathers riches cannot ascend to heaven. As a fresh wound is more easily healed,
so old wounds of the soul are hard to heal,
and are healed only with toil, even if they are healed. As it is impossible for a dead person to walk,
so it is impossible for one who has cut off hope of his life [?]. As one who says, "I have true faith," and commits sin,
he is like a face that has no eyes. He who does not have true faith and performs ascetic labors is like a man who draws up water
and pours it into a pierced jar. As a ship that has a good master over its sailors enters harbor in peace, so a soul that has a good shepherd will ascend to heaven in peace, with the help of God,
if it is obedient, even if it has committed many sins. As one who travels an unknown road without a guide easily goes astray, even if he is intelligent, so he who by his own authority,

and walks according to his own will, in the monastic life he will easily perish from the very beginning, even if he possesses all the wisdom of the world. If someone is weak in the flesh and has committed many sins, let him walk the way of humility and of its works,

for otherwise he will not find life. Just as it is impossible for someone who has been sick for a long time to return in a single moment to his former strength and health, so it is impossible for a man subject to passions to destroy his passions completely in an instant. Of every passion and virtue that you have, learn its measure, and watch constantly when it grows and when it diminishes, and in this way you will know its progress and its measure.
Just as those who exchange gold for clay suffer great loss, so too do those who display their spiritual virtues for the sake of bodily honor. Many have quickly obtained forgiveness of sins,
but no one has quickly acquired freedom from passion, for this requires the help of God, length of time, and much labor. Let us take heed

which beasts or birds attack our field at the time of sowing, which at the time of sprouting, and which at the time of harvest, so that we may properly set up snares and lay traps for them. Just as it is improper,

if a [?] (literally "head-and-neck") lies upon someone, for him to kill himself, so too it is evil to cut off hope, even up to the point of death. Just as it is a disgrace if someone buries his father and, on returning from the burial, immediately holds a wedding,
so it is improper for those who mourn for their sins to seek from people in this passing world honor, or rest,
or glory. Just as the dwelling of rulers is one thing and that of the condemned is another, so those who have sinned must take up a changed and hard way of working and living,

and not one like that of the sinless. Just as a king does not disregard a soldier whose face has been wounded in battle, but gives him gifts and honor, so the eternal King Christ will crown with the crown of joy the monk who is beset by many afflictions and trials in the battle with the demons.
Wisdom is in the soul by nature, but sin destroys that wisdom. Knowledge of evil begets ceasing from it,

and knowledge is the offspring of conscience, which is the mind that knows good and evil. Conscience has been given to us by God as a reprover concerning evil deeds and as our guardian, and it is strengthened in us by baptism. The more it is purified, the more able it is to reprove, and the more it is trampled down, the weaker it grows;
therefore it does not reprove the unbaptized strongly concerning evil, but only weakly;
but those among the baptized who listen to it, it causes to cease from evil deeds. Ceasing from evil deeds begets hatred of them, and hatred of evil is the beginning of repentance.
And the beginning of repentance is the beginning of life and the purifier of the mind, and the purification of the mind is the begetter of ascetic struggle,
and ascetic struggle is the beginning of the virtues, and the beginning of the virtues is the flower of the soul. And fear begets the keeping of the commandments.

And the keeping of the commandments is the image of love; and the beginning of love is the increase of humility, and the abundance of humility is the mother of impassibility; and the acquisition of impassibility is the perfection of love; and the perfection of love is the indwelling of God, through impassibility, in those who are pure in heart. To him belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

Discourse of our holy father John, on the stillness of body and soul. Chapter 27. For since we have become slaves of those unclean passions and obedient to them, we therefore also know a little of the wiles and devices and deeds of the evil spirits that have mastered this wretched soul of ours. But there are others who, by the power of the Holy Spirit and by complete liberation from them, know their devices. For it is one thing for someone, from the pains and agonies of sickness, to perceive what rest health holds; and it is another for someone, from the joy of health, to perceive and depict the sorrow of illness. So now we, being weak, are afraid to speak wisdom to you about that harbor of stillness.

For I know that, just as a dog stands by the table and watches for a chance to snatch bread and eat it by itself, so the devil stands by the good community of obedient brothers. And he strives to snatch a soul away from it on the pretext of stillness, to find it alone, without a helper, and to devour it. For this reason, then, so that we may not give him an opening through this word of ours, nor a pretext to those who seek a pretext, I have until now not thought it right to speak of peace and tranquility to those who are in battle, the soldiers of the heavenly King.

But this only we say: that for those who fight well, a crown of peace and stillness is made ready. And now, if you wish, let us say some small thing by way of understanding, so that no one may be grieved if we leave the discussion of this matter entirely unexamined. Stillness of the body is the calming of habits and senses; and stillness of the soul is the understanding of one's thoughts and a mind that cannot be robbed. A brave and valiant thought is the friend of stillness, which stands at the doors of the heart unceasingly,

and sleeplessly, and of the enemies who approach, some it kills and some it drives away. Whoever has become still with understanding of heart knows this saying; but whoever is still an infant is ignorant of it and has not seen its taste. For the solitary who has understanding, words are of no use, for by deeds he is enlightened about words as well. The beginning of stillness is this: to flee from the voices and tumults of the people as things that disturb the mind. And its end is this: not to fear that the tumults and voices of the people may disturb one's calm, but to be wholly impassible among them. Whoever becomes still for the sake of understanding will be instructed and will become a house of love, and he will be wholly gentle and unmoved toward contradiction and anger; but whoever does not sit with understanding will become a slave of anger and pride.
The solitary is the one who confines the bodiless and immaterial mind within a material cell: this is a wondrous and great deed. The one who searches for it seeks the pearl;

but that invisible pearl is the mind of the solitary. If the parable spoken above seems contemptible to you, then you have not yet come to know stillness. This is not for just any monk, for one who is alone needs great caution and a mind that cannot be stolen away. A neighbor often helps the one who lives with others, but an angel helps the one who lives alone. The manifest powers of the angels help and dwell with the spiritual solitary; but the opposite of this I will pass over in silence and not speak of. The abyss of divine matters is deep, and the mind of the solitary dwells in it. It is hardly safe to swim in clothes, and theology is no peace for one subject to passion. The cell of the solitary is the wall of the body, and the body of the solitary is the wall of the mind, and within it holds the house of understanding. Whoever has passion and spiritual sickness and undertakes stillness is like a man who throws himself from a boat into the heart of the sea with a small plank in his hands and wishes to reach land without toil.
For those who struggle against this flesh of clay, stillness is good at its proper time, if they also have a guide, for complete solitude requires angelic strength. My word concerns true solitaries,

who are still in spirit and in body. The despondent solitary tells lies and invites people with some story [lit. parable], so that they may bring him out of stillness. When he leaves his cell he blames the demons, and does not understand that he himself has become a demon to himself. I have seen solitaries whose blazing desire for God, like fire, was brought through stillness to an unending fulfillment, and they begot fire from fire, love from love, and desire from desire. The solitary is a true image of an angel on earth, and on the parchment of desire for God, with the writing of zeal, he has set his prayer free from all sloth and despondency. The solitary is the one who cries out in truth: "Always" [?]. The solitary is the one who has said: "Shut, beloved, the door of the cell on the body, shut the door of the tongue on speech, and shut the door of the heart on those evil spirits." The stillness of the sea and the heat of the sun test the patience of the sailor, and the lack of necessities reveals the patience of the solitary.
When a sailor grows despondent he swims in the waters; and the solitary becomes fainthearted when he mixes with the crowd. Do not be afraid of apparitions and voices, for mourning knows no vain fear,

nor is he terrified by illusions. He whose mind has learned true prayer speaks to the Lord face to face, like a man who converses with a king ear to ear; but he who prays only with words, in a bodily way, is like a man who falls down before the king in the presence of all the princes; and those who are among lay people are like men who entreat him amid the tumult of all the people. If you have learned this art well, you are not ignorant of what has been said. Sit as a guard over the thoughts of your heart. If only you know how to keep watch, and look carefully, then you will learn how, or when, or from where, or how many enter your vineyard to steal. When you grow weary from watching and spying, get up and pray, and then sit down again to your work courageously. Someone very experienced in this wished to say a little on the subject, but he was afraid: lest slackness should beguile even the laborer, and lest he should turn back with the terror of his words those who were desiring to enter upon it. Whoever speaks of stillness, let him speak sparingly and with understanding: the demons grow enraged against him, for no one so exposes their foulness as he does. He who has reached the perfection of stillness,

knows the depth of the mysteries; but he does not arrive there unless he first endures the tumults of the waves, and the fierceness of the winds and their assaults. The apostle Paul confirms this saying, for if he had not been caught up to paradise through stillness, he would not have heard the unutterable words. The ears of stillness will hear wondrous things from God, for in Job too this all-wise stillness spoke. The solitary is he who flees from people, without hatred, in the same way that the faint-hearted and slothful person flees to people, but who flees for this reason: that the sweetness of God may not be ruined within him. Go, for selling requires time, but scatter it also to the monks, so that by prayer they may help you toward stillness, burdened as you are by obedience; and bear mightily the weight of the slaying of the passions, and [?] to blessed stillness, and I will teach you visibly the work and way of life of the invisible powers. Those heavenly ones are not sated forever and ever with praising the Creator, nor will those who have been in that heaven of stillness be sated with glorifying the Maker. Those bodiless ones have no care at all for what is bodily; nor do those bodily bodiless ones care for necessities. The former have no desire for
tastes; nor do the latter have desire for any human necessity,

or for the sake of bodily rest. The heavenly ones do not concern themselves with possessions; nor do these concern themselves with wickedness and the warfare of the demons. Among the heavenly ones there is no desire for visible creatures; nor among these is there lust for faces. The heavenly ones never cease advancing in the love of God; nor do these cease imitating them. The wealth of their advancement is not unknown to them; nor to these is the passionate longing for ascent to heaven. The heavenly ones do not cease until they reach the seraphim; nor do these until they become angels. Blessed is the one who has the hope of attaining this measure; thrice blessed is the one who has drawn near to it; and an angel is the one who has attained it. On the various kinds of solitary stillness. This too is known to all: that in all works and arts there are differences of will, intention, and measure. For not all have the perfect measure; some have the perfect and others an inferior one, either from their weakness or from their sloth, and for this reason there are differences in this work also. For some enter this harbor, or rather this abyss, because of the weakness of their flesh and faces and the tyranny of their habits, in order to cut these off; and others because they were wrathful, and

the wretched ones could not overcome their anger among people. Others, out of their own self-esteem and pride, wished to enter this sea. Others entered into it because, while living among material things, they could not detach themselves from material things. Others did so in order to acquire diligence through solitude. Others chose it in order to punish themselves in secret for their sins. And others entered into it in order to bring themselves glory from people. But there are others (if only, when the Son of Man comes upon the earth, such as these are found) who out of desire for and thirst after the love of God have joined themselves to this blessed state, since before entering it they gave a bill of divorce to every thought of despondency; for to dwell with despondency is separation from that first [love?]. According to this small wisdom which was given to me, as to an ignorant master-builder, I have hewn out a ladder; and now let each one see on which rung of this ladder of the solitaries he stands. The first rung is for the sake of self-esteem; the second for the sake of glory from people; the third from weakness of the tongue; the fourth for the sake of flight from material things; the fifth because of the tyranny of anger; the sixth so that they may punish themselves; the seventh so that they may acquire diligence;

the eighth so that they may add fire to fire. Those seven rungs are the works of this sevenfold present world, some of them good and some evil, while the eighth foreshadows the age to come. Keep watch, O solitary monk, at the time when the beasts come; otherwise you will not be able to set the trap well.

If the one who received the letter of separation by hand has departed, handiwork is superfluous; but if he is not yet separated, I do not know how I should remain in stillness. Why did not as many luminaries appear from those holy Tabennesiots as appeared from the monks of Scetis? He who understands, let him understand, for I am not able to say it, and even more, I do not wish to. Some by battling and resisting the passions; and some by chanting, spending the greater part of the time in psalmody; and some by standing in prayer; and others by being in contemplation, pass their hours in these ways. Examine also what was said above, and whoever understands by the Lord's help, let him understand. There are slothful souls who entered the community of a monastery, found food in abundance as an aid to their laxity, and came to complete perdition;

and there are others who stripped off their laxity by living with others; and this has often happened in the same way not only to the slothful, but also to the zealous. By the same rule we say concerning stillness too that it has received many experienced men and made them inexperienced, and through self-will has exposed their love of pleasure; and it has taken others and, through fear and concern for bearing their own judgment, has made them zealous and fervent. Let no one overcome by anger and pride, by duplicity and rancor, seek to see even a trace of stillness, lest he acquire only straying of the mind; but he who is pure of these,

he himself will know what is better, and I think that not even he will know all of it. Those who practice stillness as is fitting, these are their signs: a sleepless mind, a pure heart, rapture toward God, keeping judgment before the eyes, remembrance of death, insatiability in prayer, a watchfulness that cannot be stolen, the mortification of fornication, ignorance of vainglory, death to the world, hatred of gluttony; a source of speaking about God,

a spring of understanding, perpetual tears, the destruction of much talking, and other things like these, whose multitude resists [?]; but those who practice it not as is fitting, this is the form of their poverty: growth of anger, storing up of rancor, the wasting away of love, increase of pride, and the rest I will pass over in silence. Since this discourse has come to such a subject, it is good that we also speak about the truly obedient, what their forms and signs are, for the discourse is addressed especially to them. Those who are in obedience lawfully, well, and fittingly, these are their signs, according to the word of the holy Fathers: daily growth of that humility of the novices, weakening of anger, the vanishing of darkness, deliverance from the passions, freedom from hatred, the blotting out of the desire [arising] from rebukes and disgraces, ignorance of despondency, increase of zeal;
love of mercy, estrangement from arrogance, which of all these [?]

[?] by [?] it is sought, and by few it is found. When there is no water in a spring, its name is empty, and what follows from this the prudent will understand. The soul that does not keep the covenant it made with the Lord defiles itself, and these works of filth follow it: forgetfulness of death, gluttony of the belly, failure to restrain the eyes, the labor of vainglory, insatiable sleep, hardness of heart, mercilessness, a treasury of evil thoughts, the multiplying of passions, captivity of the heart, an abundance of turmoil, disobedience, contentiousness, vain love, unbelief, impropriety, much talking, and boldness, the worst of all; and more grievous than all is hardness of heart, which is followed by fearlessness toward God, which is the mother of all falls and passions. Of solitaries [?], but of those living in obedience, three [?]. The solitary who is dominated by despondency,

will be greatly distressed, for the hours of prayer and contemplation are wasted in the battle against it. Once I grew weary of staying in my cell and became fainthearted, so much that I wanted to abandon it. And as I was about to go out from there, some men came and called me blessed as a solitary, and immediately that thought of despondency was driven away by vainglory, and I marveled at how that demon of pride, resembling a bull's head, overcomes all the demons.

Set your mind at every hour to examining your scales: from which side they tilt, at the time of turning back, and again at the time of tilting and of leveling, and see to what point and from what direction the tilt and the victory are greater. But whoever has acquired stillness through the Holy Spirit knows this saying. The first work of stillness above all is freedom from care about affairs, both proper and improper, for whoever opens the door to the former will undoubtedly be seized by the latter. The second work of stillness is prayer removed from all negligence; the third is the unrobbed contemplation of the heart. Just as it is impossible for one who has not learned to join letters together to read books as well, so it is impossible for those who have not acquired the first to perform properly these two that follow. I was [?]

I reached [?], and they illumined the thirsty one, and behold, I was among them. But what its former visible color was, I could not learn, for the ruler did not wish it. Yet I asked to know how it is now, and he told me that it is in its own [state]. But I only said, "What is the upright standing and the sitting of that ailment [?]?" And he said that it is impossible to speak of this to the ears. Then I asked about what I longed for, and he said that the time has not yet come to hear about such a deficiency [?] of that fire of incorruption. Whether this was with this earth I do not know, or whether without it, I am altogether ignorant.

It is hard to drive away [?] by sleep at that midday hour, especially in the days of summer, and only then is handiwork good. I saw the demon of despondency, how it outruns and runs ahead of the demon of fornication, in order to loosen the flesh and sink it in sleep, and in this way bring defilements upon solitaries. If you resist them, they will fight you powerfully and fiercely, so that you may say, "It profits me nothing," and thus cease from ascetic struggle,

But be courageous; for nothing so reveals the defeat of the demons as their battles against us. When the time comes to go out from your cell, guard firmly what has been gathered within the cell; for when the door is opened, those confined birds quickly fly away, and the benefit of stillness vanishes. A small hair troubles the eye, and a small care ruins stillness; for stillness is the gathering in of the mind and the putting away even of proper cares and concerns. Whoever has acquired true stillness does not care even for his own body, for He who promised is unfailing. Whoever wishes to present his mind pure before the Lord yet multiplies his cares is like a man who binds his feet tightly and wishes to run swiftly. Some say that it is difficult to learn all philosophical teaching, and that few are found who do; but I say that it is far more difficult, and that few are found who know that wisdom of stillness.

Whoever has not known God as is proper is entirely inexperienced in stillness, and many waves come upon him. Stillness afflicts the inexperienced, for since he has not seen the taste of the sweetness of God, with despondency and captivity of mind,

and with every kind of thought he passes his hours. Whoever, from the multitude [?], like a wild ass [?]; for what else has healed that wild ass gone savage, except prayer? He over whom the passions have gained mastery dwells in the desert being trained by them, as a holy elder told me: I mean George Arselaites, who is not unknown to your honor also. He taught this poor soul of mine about stillness and said: "I set my mind to observe, and I saw the demons of vainglory and lust coming at dawn, and at midday those of despondency, grief and anger, and in the evening those dung-lovers, the demons of gluttony, arrive." A poor disciple is better than a solitary who lives amid cares. Whoever lives in stillness and does not perceive benefit day by day, know that either he is not doing the works of stillness, or he is being taken captive by pride. Stillness is unceasing standing before God, and service of Him.

Let the remembrance of the Lord Jesus stay with you as your breath does, and then you will know the benefit of stillness. The fall of a disciple is his own will, and the fall of a solitary is the ruin of prayer. If you rejoice at the arrival of guests, know that you are joined to despondency and not to God. As an image of prayer, take that widow who was afflicted by her adversary; and the image of stillness is the great solitary Arsenius, the equal of the angels. Remember, O you who live alone, the conduct of this angelic solitary, and see how many times he turned away even those who had come to him, so as not to lose what was greater. I saw demons who, as was fitting [?], sent wandering and negligent monks to solitaries, so that by this means they might hinder those workers of virtue at least a little. Learn to recognize such people, O true solitary, and do not shrink from distressing them with the fear of God; perhaps they will be ashamed and cease from their wandering about. Beware lest, on account of this example mentioned above, you distress in vain a soul that comes to you thirsting to draw up water; but in all things the lamp of discernment is needful for you. Let the life of solitaries, and still more of all monks, be lived with understanding and the witness of conscience. He who lives according to the rule, all his deeds and words and the thoughts of his heart
and impulses he should do according to the will of the Lord, and for the Lord, with understanding of soul and with beholding the face of the Lord; but if he goes astray,

he is not living according to the rule at all. The prophet says something, but I say: I will tell my will to the Lord in prayer, and from him I will receive full assurance. Faith is the wing of prayer,
for if prayer does not have it, it will return again to our bosom [?]. Faith is the standing of the soul without doubting,
so that it may not be shaken by any opposing wind. A believer is not the one who believes that God can do this,
but the one who believes, 'My request will surely be given to me.' Faith obtains [?] things beyond hope, and the thief showed this. The mother of faith is diligence and a sincere heart,
for the one makes a person free of doubt, and the other fulfills the request in deed. The mother of solitaries is faith,
for if he does not believe, how could he live well in stillness? Those who are bound in prison tremble for fear of the judge,
but he who lives in stillness in a cell wastes away for fear of the Lord. The first does not so fear the court
as the second fears the judgment of Christ. Acquire the fear of the Lord mightily in stillness, O beloved,
for nothing drives out despondency as it does. The condemned man in prison watches for when

[?] the judge will come, but the true solitary [considers] when death will come. The former is bound by sorrow, and the latter by a fountain of tears. If you have acquired the staff of patience, the powers of despondency will depart from you. Patience is the sinew and strength of the soul, which does not fall because of afflictions and battles. The patient person is a worker who does not fall, and if he does fall, he conquers even by falling. Patience is the daily expectation of trials. Patience is the destroyer of excuses and the guarding of oneself. As this nature of ours necessarily needs food, so the solitary needs patience. The latter is a cause of being crowned, while the former often becomes a cause of passions. The monk is dead before burial, and his tomb is his cell. Patience is born of hope and mourning, for whoever is apart from these two is a slave of despondency. The soldier of Christ ought to know from which enemies he must flee at a distance, and which he must let come near and fight hand to hand. Sometimes battle plaits a crown, and sometimes withdrawal from battle leaves a person untested. These rules cannot be taught by words, for we are not all at one level, nor do we have equal battles. One [?]
[?] he fights you unceasingly, in standing and walking, in sitting and lying down,

and in prayer and in sleep. Not that they call to mind with one thought of the heart [?]; for some have this as their exercise, that [?]; and others have this, that [?]; and others exercise themselves in this, that [?]; and others ponder this, that [?]; and others ponder, that [?]; and others exercise themselves, that [?]; and others ponder that saying, that without labor [?] a crown. Whoever is advancing well toward perfection does his own work not only when he is awake but even in sleep; for this reason some battle demons and conquer them even in sleep. Do not expect guests or prepare in advance for their coming, for the rule of the solitary is simple and sincere. No one is able to build that tower of solitude unless he first sits down and reckons whether he has the materials for building it;

lest after laying the foundation he become a laughingstock to his enemies and a stumbling block to other workers who do good. Examine well the sweetness that comes to you in the time of solitude, lest it be from bitter physicians, or rather from murderous enemies. At night give the greater part of the time to prayer and a little to psalmody, and again by day arrange things according to your strength. The reading of books does no small amount to gather and enlighten the mind, for they are the words of the Holy Spirit, and they strengthen those who read them. Read the books that speak about virtues and passions,

and everything that instructs your life, so that it may gather well in your mind. Seek to find the words of life from labors rather than from books. Do not read the thoughts of those in error before you reach great perfection, for they are words of darkness and they darken the weak. By one drink the taste of wine is known, and by one word all the inner work of the hesychast becomes recognizable to knowledgeable teachers. Fight with all your strength against pride, for nothing is a worse robber of the mind than it. Guard your tongue when you go out of your cell, for it can quickly scatter many labors. Acquire a simple way of life, for crookedness defiles

stillness. For those who come to you, set out whatever is fitting, whether bodily or spiritual. If they are wiser than we are, let us show wisdom by silence; if they are our equals in measure, let us open the door; yet it is good to count everyone as higher than ourselves. The power of a king is a multitude of people and of riches, and the power of hesychasts is abundant prayer. Just as the confession of the holy, uncreated and worshipful Trinity and the confession of the bodily dispensation of one of that same holy Trinity are opposed in their wording;

for what is spoken of there as divided is spoken of here as one, and what is spoken of there as one is spoken of here as divided, since there we say three persons and one nature, and here one person and two natures; so too the works of stillness are one thing and the works of obedience another. The holy prophet and the holy apostle say that [?], but I say: who has known the mind of a man truly still in body and soul, by the power of the Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. The might of a king consists of wealth and many subjects, and likewise the might of the hesychast consists of abundance of prayer.

Spoken by the same, concerning all-holy prayer, the mother of virtues, and concerning standing well in it in body and mind. Chapter 28. Prayer by nature is the union of God and man, and in action it is the sustaining of the world and reconciliation with God; the mother of tears and in turn their child; the forgiver of sins; a bridge over trials and a wall between us and afflictions; the crusher of battles, the work of angels and the food of the bodiless powers; the joy of the age to come, a work without end, the spring of virtues, the leader of graces, invisible progress,

and food of the soul, light of the mind, slayer of despair and cause of hope, deliverer from sorrow, wealth of monks and treasury of hesychasts, dispeller of anger, mirror of perfection, revealer of one's measure, image of right order, foreteller of the age to come, and sign of courage. For the true man of prayer, prayer is a tribunal and a judgment seat before that great judgment. Let us rise and listen to this blessed queen of the virtues, to the voice with which she cries out to us, saying in a loud voice: [?] and consolation

of your wounds, and physician of the great diseases of sin. All of us who go to meet God and our King, let us not make that journey unprepared, lest he see us from afar unarmed and naked of royal adornment, and command his servants to drive us far from his face, bound, and our written petitions be returned torn to our very faces. When you go to stand before the Lord, let the garment of your soul be woven with the [?] ("heel-piece"; perhaps "thread") of not remembering wrongs; otherwise you will gain nothing from prayer. Let all your asking be made with a humble mind, for the publican and the prodigal became pleasing to God by a single word. Standing before God in prayer has one form, but many divisions,

and each of its kinds is distinct. Some speak as to a friend and King, interceding for others and no longer for themselves; others ask for glory and spiritual riches and greater boldness; others implore to be delivered from their adversary; others seek to receive honor; others pray for complete release from their debt; others fall down in supplication for release from prison, and others for forgiveness of sins. Before everything else, on the chart of our petition let us set thanksgiving, and second, confession and contrition of heart with understanding, and only then let us make our request known to the King; for this is the good form of prayer, as was made known to a certain brother

by an angel. If you have ever stood before a visible judge, you will need no other model for how to stand in your prayer. But if you have neither stood there yourself nor seen others standing, then take this model at least from the sick person, how he implores the physician when he is about to cut or burn him. Do not speak with philosophical wisdom in prayer, for many times tender young children, by simple words, have made their Father in heaven merciful toward them. Do not seek much speaking, so that your mind may not be scattered in searching for words;

for one word of the publican made God merciful, and one word of faith saved the thief. Much speaking has many times scattered the mind, but saying even one word fervently gathers it together. When you are moved to compunction at some word in prayer, stay on it and say it many times, for our guardian prays near us and with us. Do not show boldness in prayer, even if you have great purity, but rather approach with great humility, and you will become all the more bold. Even if you have climbed the whole ladder of virtues, still pray for forgiveness of sins; for you hear what Paul, that great apostle, says about sinners, that [?]. Oil and salt are the seasoners of food, and what gives wings to prayer is purity and

...tears. If you clothe yourself wholly in meekness and freedom from anger, you will not have to labor much to free your mind from captivity. Until we acquire pure and proper prayer, know that we are like small children who are able to see well [?]. Strive to lift up your mind and to confine it within the words of your prayer; and if it grows weak because of its immaturity and sinks low, raise it up again. Instability is proper to the mind, but he is able to restrain it,

who can do all things: God. O beloved, if you struggle well, he will come upon you too who hedges in the sea of the mind, and he will say [?]. It is impossible to bind a spirit, but where the Creator of the spirit is, all things obey him. If you have seen the sun, you can speak about it; but what you have not seen, how can you speak of it without falsehood? The beginning of prayer is that thoughts come only in small measure and are easily driven away; the middle is that the mind be only in the words; and its perfection is the love of God. One thing is the joy of prayer that occurs among the obedient, and another is that which occurs among solitaries; for in the first there may perhaps arise even the illusion of arrogance, while the second is full of humility.

If you always teach your mind not to depart from you, it will be with you even at the table, when it is being laid; but if you accustom it to roam about unrestrained, it will never come to you. The great laborer of true prayer, Paul, says that in church [?]; but this is far from those who are infants in mind, for along with our gathering of the mind, quantity of prayer is also needful; and this second is the bringer [?] of the first, as Scripture says, that he will grant also what is pure [?], with toil and hardship, to the one who entreats him. One thing is the defilement of prayer,

another is corruption, another is theft, and another is blemish. Defilement is when a person stands before the Lord and occupies himself with evil thoughts; corruption is when, at the time of prayer, he is carried off captive to unprofitable cares; theft is when the mind wanders about without his noticing; and blemish is any vain thought that comes to us at that time. If we are not alone at the time of prayer, let us form the posture of supplication inwardly; but if those servants of praise are not with us, then let us make supplication with outward posture as well, for in many ways the mind is joined with the body in those who are not yet perfect. All who approach the King need contrition of heart, but above all those who ask for remission of debts and forgiveness of sins. If we are still in prison,

let us listen to him who says to Peter: Arise, wrap about you the garment of obedience, strip off your own will, and, naked of it, look to the Lord in your prayer, and call upon his will alone; and then you will find God holding the rudders of your soul, and he will steer your life without its sinking. Arise from love of the world and love of pleasure.

Cast away cares, deny your flesh, and strip off the thoughts of the heart, for prayer is nothing other than the renunciation of the world, both visible and invisible, as that speaker says: [?] "but only this, that I may always be nailed to you." To some, wealth seems good, to others glory, and to others honor; of dispassion [?]. Faith gives prayer wings, for without it prayer cannot ascend to heaven. Although that judge does not fear God, for he himself is God, yet because of the trouble caused him by the soul widowed from the good through falling into sins, he will give her justice against her adversaries, the flesh, and against the demons who fight her. Let us who are subject to the passions not cease entreating the Lord, for all the dispassionate have attained dispassion from a state of passion. Our good Lord draws grateful and good souls to his love by granting their requests quickly, but the ungrateful

and unperceptive he does not grant quickly, so that by hunger and thirst for what they ask he may make them persevere in prayer, always entreating him. For when a dog receives bread it goes off, away from the one who gave it;

and when a foolish and unperceptive soul receives what it asked for, it no longer falls down before God in entreaty. Do not say, "I have spent much time in prayer and have achieved nothing," for look, you are achieving something already: you stand before the Lord and converse with him. For what higher good could there be than standing before the Lord and being united with him through prayer? A man under condemnation does not fear the sentence of his punishment as much as one who struggles fears at prayer that it may harm him. Therefore, if he is wise and prudent, through this concern he will wipe away from himself all slander, and care, and contention, and grief, and satiety. Prepare your soul beforehand by prayer, ahead of the time of prayer and of your entreaty to God, and you will soon prosper well. I saw men who shone in obedience and who, as far as was possible, did not neglect the remembrance of God in their minds; the moment they stood for prayer they swiftly mastered their minds, and streams of tears flowed like rivers, for they had been prepared beforehand through obedience. Psalmody with many people brings distraction of the mind, whereas solitary psalmody does not bring so much distraction of the mind; but then solitary psalmody is assailed by despondency, while with many people there is zeal

[?] helps. The love of a soldier for his king is shown by battle on his behalf, and the love of a monk for God is shown by the time of prayer. Your prayer will reveal your measure and your deeds to you, for the holy fathers have named it the mirror of the monk. Whoever is occupied with some task at the time of prayer, the demons make sport of him, for this is the will of those demons: to steal away from us one hour after another. Do not disregard someone who begs you, "Pray for me," even if you do not have perfect prayer; rather, pray for him with a contrite heart, for the faith of the one who asks many times with contrition has saved the one praying as well. Take care not to become proud when you pray for others and the Lord hears your prayer; rather, know that it was because of their faith that the Lord granted that grace. Every teacher demands from a child each day the recitation of what he has learned, and the Lord will demand from every mind, day by day in prayer, the power it has received from God. When you pray well,

then the battles of the enemies will rise up against you, for this is always their custom. Every virtue, and prayer above all, should be practiced with understanding and with fervor of heart. The soul prays fervently when it has overcome anger. Every thing gained by much asking and labor

and by time is firm. Whoever has gained the Lord within himself has no need to be taught prayer by word, for then the Holy Spirit himself is his intercessor with his own self. Do not accept any visible fantasy or vision in prayer, lest madness come upon you and your mind be led astray. The assurance of every request appears in prayer. Assurance is freedom from all doubt. Assurance is unwavering knowledge of unknown things. Be [?] of holy prayer, for by it monks [?] but the latter with the latter. When the fire of fervor is kindled in the soul, then prayer rises up and ascends, and when prayer rises up and is lifted to heaven, there comes a descent of that divine light into the upper chamber of the soul. Some say that prayer is higher than the remembrance of death, but I glorify one person with two natures. A good horse, when it goes on and warms up, adds all the more to its running; and by running I understand

the singing of prayer, and by the horse the courageous mind. Such a one perceives the spirit of battle from afar, and having prepared in advance he stands unconquered forever. It is harsh for a thirsty man to have water snatched from his mouth, and how much harsher it is for a zealous monk who is praying with compunction if someone should interrupt that longed-for prayer before its completion. Do not [?] until you see the fire and the water turned back to you again, for you may perhaps not find another such time for the forgiveness of your sins in all your days. Whoever has seen the taste of prayer defiles his mind by saying a single word, many times over; and when he goes to prayer, he does not find that longed-for sweetness as he usually does. It is another thing to have oversight of the heart by the mind, the ruler and chief priest who offers those rational sacrifices to Christ.

Upon some who approach it, that holy fire of heaven burns them, as one of the theologians says; it burns them because of their deficiency in purity. And others it illumines, because of their measure of perfection, for the same is called both burning fire and purifying light. For this reason some come out from prayer as from a furnace, purified of the matter of sins; and others come out from it as those illumined by light and clothed with the heavenly [?] of humility and joys.

But those who come out of prayer without either of these two states have prayed as though bodily and not spiritually. If bodies that touch another's body have the appearance and condition of their nature changed, then how shall he not be changed who touches the body of God with innocent hands? Something like the ways of the kings of the earth is seen also with that good King of ours: for sometimes he himself, sometimes through his friend, sometimes through a servant, and sometimes in an entirely hidden way, he bestows his gifts on his soldiers; but he multiplies his graces toward us according to our humility. Just as it is abhorrent to an earthly king if someone stands before him and turns his face away and converses with the king's enemies, so also it is abhorrent

before the Lord when someone stands in prayer and entertains impure thoughts. When that dog, the plunderer of the mind, comes upon you, drive it away with the weapon of prayer, and however many times it grows fierce, do not give up and do not give it place. Ask with mourning, seek with obedience, and knock with long-suffering.

For he who thus [?]. Be on your guard, and do not pray very much for a woman during prayer, lest you be taken captive from the right side. Do not begin, in prayer, to confess your bodily sins as they happened to you, lest you become your own murderer. Do not make the time of prayer a time for examining and training in spiritual matters; otherwise that higher thing will be withheld from you [?]. He who unceasingly holds the staff of prayer will not stumble, and even if something should happen and he stumbles, he will not fall completely, for prayer is a wondrous thing, divine and sweet, which does not let a person go toward evil. From this we recognize its great benefit,
for nowhere do the enemies fight us so much

as in prayer; and we shall know its fruit when our enemies are utterly defeated, for by this we shall know that at the time of battle [?]. The psalmist says, that is, with mouth and soul and mind, for in whatever prayer there are gathered

soul and mind together [?]. Neither bodily nor spiritual forms are the same for all, for to some the prayer of psalmody comes sooner and to others later; for the former against the captivity of the mind;

and the latter fight against lack of learning. If you unceasingly entreat the Master concerning your enemies, then when they draw near you, be bold of heart. You will not labor much, but they will flee from you of their own accord, for those impure ones do not wish it when they see that you receive a crown through battle with them; rather, beaten by prayer, they flee as from fire. Acquire good courage for yourself,
And in this way you will gain God as your teacher of prayer. Just as the sight of the eyes is not taught by words, for it is natural,
so too the beauty of prayer is not taught by another's words, for it has God as its instructor;

it is not a matter of words, that you might hear and learn them, or the excellence of a craft, that you might receive it from someone else. Rather, God is its instructor, who teaches people knowledge, grants the petition of those who pray to him, and blesses the years of the righteous; for his is the glory, now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.
Discourse of the same on dispassion and perfection and the resurrection of the soul before the resurrection of all. Chapter 29. Behold, we too, lying in that deep cave of unintelligence,
and amid the dark passions and these shadows of the death of the flesh, boldly begin to speak of this lofty firmament, which is dispassion.
The visible firmament of heaven has the stars as its adornment, and dispassion has the virtues; for I understand dispassion to be nothing other than a heaven of the heart and mind,

which counts all the battles of the devil as a mere breeze. The truly dispassionate person is the one whose flesh has become free of passion and wholly incorruptible, whose mind has been raised above created things, to whom all the senses have been made subject, who has presented his soul before the face of the Lord, and who always goes toward him even beyond his own strength. Again, some say that dispassion is the resurrection of the soul before the resurrection of the body; and others say that dispassion is [?] of God equal to that of the angels, or only slightly less than theirs.

That perfect, unending perfection of the perfect, when it comes to a person, as someone who had tasted it told me, so purifies the mind and so snatches it away from the material things of the world, that for the greater part of his life that companion of it, caught up from the world, passes his time in the harbor of heavenly vision.

Concerning this, the one who had tasted it said: Such was that Egyptian, who did not dare to hold his hands raised to heaven for long when he prayed with others, lest he forget where he was and not come back there for a long time. There is a dispassionate person, and there is another more dispassionate than the dispassionate; for the one strongly hates evil things, while the other is always exceedingly rich in virtues. The purity of virginity, too, is called dispassion, and rightly, for it is the forerunner of the resurrection of all and of the incorruption of those corruptible natures. He showed dispassion who said, "I have the mind of the Lord." That Egyptian showed dispassion who said, "I do not fear the Lord." He showed dispassion who prayed that it might return [?]
Who in this present life, before that age to come, gained such dispassion and perfection as that Syrian?
For David, that renowned and great one among the prophets, said to the Lord: [?];
but this great striver for the Lord said: "Calm, O Lord, the waves of your grace." That soul has dispassion,

who would be as fervent for the virtues as those who are enslaved by passion are for their lusts. If this is the limit of gluttony, that even when a man has no wish to eat he forces himself to eat, then surely this is the limit of fasting, that he does not give food to his hungry nature even though it is blameless. If this is the unnatural limit of the love of fornication, that a man is moved by passion even toward animals and lifeless objects, then surely this is the limit of perfect purity, that with regard to all passion he looks on everyone as on lifeless things. If this is the end of the love of silver, that a man never ceases from gathering and is never satisfied by it, then surely this is the perfection of poverty, that he does not spare even his own flesh. If this is the greatness of despondency, that a man has no patience even in rest, then surely this is patience, that he counts affliction as patience. If this is the depth of anger, that a man grows angry even when he is alone, then surely this is the work of long-suffering, that he looks on the one who distresses him as on a friend. If this is the height of vainglory, that even if no one is with him to praise him, he

still performs deeds of display, then surely this is the form of humility, that even among people the mind does not steal away into display. If this is the form of pride, that a man exalts himself over worthless deeds,

then surely this is the excellence of humility, that a man counts his own lofty virtues as nothing. If this is enslavement to passion, that a man follows all the thoughts sown by the demons, then surely this is the sign of that blessed dispassion, that a man can truly say: "I do not know how it came, or why, nor how it departed, but I am wholly ignorant of evil things, and I am and shall be entirely united with God always." Whoever in this very world becomes worthy of such a measure has God as his own teacher, who dwells within him,
and inwardly he hears the voice that comes from him, brilliantly, by that divine light, higher than every visible voice.

For I can no longer bear the sharpness of that longing, but I seek that beauty which he granted me before this clay. But why should anyone speak at length about dispassion? For he is no longer alive, as says the one who fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the true faith. Just as a king's crown is not adorned with a single precious stone, so also dispassion does not

[?] comes about, if even one virtue is neglected. Understand dispassion in this way: as if it were the palace of the great King, and there are many mansions in it, and its wall is the forgiveness of sins. Let us run, my brothers, I beseech you, let us run and hasten to enter that palace of the great King and that bridal chamber of joy. But if, because of the weight of sins and evil habits, we cannot enter that bridal chamber (alas for this trial!), then let us at least hasten to reach one of its mansions. And if we cannot enter even there, let us not remain outside the wall, but let us hasten by every possible means to get inside that wall. For whoever does not enter within that wall before the end will wander astray outside in the deserts and be devoured by wild beasts.

For this reason the prophet prayed, saying [?], and another prophet says, as from the mouth of God, that [?]. Let us cut through, O beloved, the middle partition of that wall, which we wickedly built through disobedience, and let us obtain here the forgiveness of debts, for there is no consolation or repentance in hell. Let us be still and understand, for we have no excuse: neither the multitude of sins, nor the weight of the burden, nor the adversity [?] of the times, nor anything else. For those who received the Lord through that washing of the second birth [?], and he said: I AM GOD, and I am dispassion

and holiness. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen. Blessed dispassion raises the mind of the poor from the dunghill of the passions and lifts it from earth to heaven, and all-praised love seats it with the princes of the angels, with the princes of the people of the Lord.

Work of the same holy father of ours, John, abbot of Sinai, on the triad, concerning the three virtues: faith, hope and love. Chapter 30. And after all these things said before, it confirms and holds fast that which is marvelous above all: of all [?], for it is called God. And I see the first as a ray, the second as light, and the third as the disc of the sun.
And all three together as one radiance and splendor. For the first is able to do all things;

and the mercy of God surrounds the second; and the third does not fall, nor does it ever cease from running, and it no longer allows the heart wounded by it to rest from that divine longing. Whoever wishes to speak about love has undertaken to speak about God, and speaking about God in words is a stumbling block for the incautious. The word of love is known only to the angels, and to them only according to the measure of their radiance. And whoever wishes to state its definition is a blind man in the abyss, counting the sand. Love by nature is likeness to God,

[?] as far as is possible and attainable for human beings; in action it is the good drunkenness of the soul, and in its character it is a fountain of faith, an abyss of long-suffering, and a sea of humility. True love is the removal of every contrary thought. Love, dispassion, and adoption as sons differ in name only, but their power is one, as with fire, flame, and light. As far as love diminishes, fear increases, for whoever has no fear is either filled with love or dead in soul. Is there anything to prevent us from adopting images of the fear of God, of diligence, of good zeal, of service, and of the love of God? Blessed is he who has acquired such a love of God as an evil lover has for his beloved. Blessed is the man who fears the Lord as those condemned by a judge fear him. Blessed is he who longs for the Lord as a hungry man longs for bread. Blessed is he who is as eager to serve the Lord as faithful servants are toward their master. Blessed is he who has such zeal for the virtues as men who love the glory of the world have for royal honors. Blessed is he who stands in prayer

before the Lord as soldiers stand in fear before the king. Blessed is he who strives to gain the favor of the Lord, as friends do with one another. Does a nursing infant long for its mother as much as a man, a son of love, longs for the Lord? Whoever has firm love and passionate desire for someone always has the face of that beloved in his imagination and holds him close with inward sweetness,
and even in sleep his longing does not fade,

but he sees that same one. So it is with fleshly beloved ones, and also with bodiless ones. Someone who was wounded by this said, and said marvelously, that because of the nature of the flesh [?], because of the abundance of love [?]. Let this be known to you, O blessed one: when the hart, which is the courageous soul, has destroyed those evil reptiles, then toward the Lord [?];

for by that fire of love they are burned, as if by a burning medicine. The working of hunger is hidden and unseen, but that of thirst is fierce, evident, and known to all. Therefore he who thirsted for God said that [?]. If the sight of a friend makes us glad, what would the sight of the face of God not do, when it comes invisibly to the pure heart? The fear of God, when it is accompanied by fervor of soul, consumes and destroys defilement, for

it says that [?]. But holy love devours some, as that speaker says that [?], and again it makes others radiant and glad, for it says that [?]. When a person is wholly mingled with the love of God, then outwardly too, as in a mirror, he displays that inner radiance of the soul, for thus was Moses, the seer of God, glorified;

And those who attain to such an angelic measure as this often forget even the food of the body. And what is surprising in this, since even evil desire has often made people forget food? So I think that the bodies of those who attain to this incorruptible measure do not fall into sicknesses in the usual way either,
for the causes of disease have perished from them,

just as the flame of fever has been quenched; nor does the food they take give them pleasure any longer, for water nourishes the root of trees, but that fire of heaven nourishes their soul. The growth of the fear of God is the beginning of love, and the end of love is the beginning of theology. He who has wholly united his senses to God has learned the mysteries of his words; for if it is not so, it is difficult to speak about God. The essential Word makes purity perfect, and his coming puts death to death; and when death has been put to death, then that disciple is enlightened

in theology. The word of the Lord abides forever and ever, but he who does not understand the Lord God as is fitting speaks by conjecture. Purity and love made that beloved disciple a theologian, who by his words confirmed the faith in the all-holy Trinity. He who loves the Lord has first come to love his brother, for the sign of the first is this second. He who loves his neighbor will never listen to slander, but will flee from it as from fire. He who says, "I love the Lord," and hates his brother is like a man who runs in his sleep. The strength of love is hope,

for through it we await the reward of love. Hope is the wealth of unknown wealth. Hope is the undoubting treasure before the treasure. Hope is rest in labors; it is the door of love; it is the crusher of despair; and it is the image of that age to come. The lack of hope is the disappearance of love, for on it depend ascetic struggles, on it hang labors, and around it stands mercy. The monk who is a worker of hope is a slayer of despondency, for he slays it with the sword of hope. The tasting of the Lord's gifts gives birth to hope, but those who have not tasted them cannot

avoid falling into doubt. Anger undoes hope, for hope is never put to shame, but anger is a matter of shame, according to the word of Solomon. Love is the head of prophecy. Love is the giver of signs. Love is an abyss of radiance. Love is a fountain of fire: the more it springs up, the more it burns the one who thirsts. Love is the firmness of angels. Love is the advancement of that age to come. Tell us, O beautiful one among the virtues, and make known to us [?]

Enlighten us and give us to drink, and lead us, and bring me up, for we long to ascend to you. For you are Lord over all. And now you have set my soul on fire, and I can no longer endure that flame of yours; therefore I will sing to you forever. Make those who love you free from battle with the proud thoughts of the heart [?]. But how did Jacob see you at the top of the ladder? I want to learn. And what is the form of the ascent of that ladder? Tell me, who long for this. Or what is the plan and arrangement of those steps, which that lover of yours [?]? Tell me. Or what is their number? I thirst to know. Or what is the time of ascending there? For the guides are known to be angels, as your beloved Jacob taught us.

And in answer to all this, the King of the virtues looked down from heaven and says in the ears of my soul: "O my lover, unless you are released from the grossness of this present world, you cannot see my beauty as it should be seen. But as for that ladder, if you ask about its steps and structures, look upon the spiritual arrangement of the virtues, and you have understood."

"And I am seated at the top of them all, and as the great Paul, the minister of my mystery, says, that [?]." A shortened instruction, which contains within itself everything that has been said at length in this book. But now let us ascend, brothers, let us ascend, for you hear the one speaking, who says, to conquer by his song [?]. Let us all run, I beg you, with the one who says, "Let us hasten" [?], who at thirty years of the visible age of his flesh received baptism, and who is seated on this thirtieth step of our spiritual ladder; for love is God, to whom belongs song, to whom
belongs steadfastness, to whom belongs power, to whom belongs every cause of good things, who was and will be, now and forever, and unto those endless good and radiant ages. Amen.
